speechtext:
House again in Committee of Supply.
Intercolonial Railway-Steel rails and fastenings, $500,000.
['We will not accept any such under this contract.\nProgress reported.\nOn motion of the Prime Minister, House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.', 'Wednesday, April 24, 1901.']

The committee. when it last had the railway estimates under consideration, had reached the first item on page 43, providing an appropriation for steel rails and fastenings. Just before the committee separated for recess on the day when I was last presenting my estimates, some statements were " made by hon. gentlemen opposite, the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the hon. leader of the opposition, to which, I think, it would be well I should make a reference before going into the particulars, or what I may call the merits of the vote. The committee will recollect that when this vote was first mentioned earlier in the debate, I explained quite fully the conditions which were attached to
the arrangement that the government had entered into. Some hon. gentlemen at the time suggested that I should bring down the contract; I said at once I would do so, and my deputy, who was here, took a minute of it, and had instructions to bring it down at the next meeting of the committee. When the committee met the next afternoon, which was the last time I was able to be present before the committee, my deputy brought the contract with him, or a copy thereof, and I immediately handed it over to the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Haggart), who desired to see it. I want the committee to note that I made my statement almost simultaneously with the assurance that I would have these papers furnished to the committee; and I felt that the gentlemen to whom I have reference would have been somewhat reluctant, at all events, in making any harsh references to what they supposed to have been misleading statements until they were assured beyond all doubt that there had been some mistake in the matter ; for if there had been a mistake you would suppose they would have been ready to assume that any member of the government would have common sense enough not to make any inaccurate statement when he was on the very eve of handing to the committee the documents and papers which would show that his statement was incorrect.
I want to refer to that statement now and I want to call the attention of the committee to the nature of the explanation I made in this regard. I said that the contract that was made with the Lake Superior Power Company was to supply rails for one year. I wished fully to apprise the committee of the facts, and I said that we had an understanding with them under which we engaged to continue the arrangement for a further term of years, the price being governed by the rate in the English market at the time when we were proposing that the arrangement should be renewed. I made that statement, Mr. Chairman, speaking from memory ; I did not refer to any papers at tlio time. I made it with the view of giving the committee all the information and without the slightest thought of withholding anything that I thought would be at all pertinent to the question, or which would be desired by the committee. I am going to ask the committee to follow me through the facts of the matter and I will leave it to the judgment of the committee as to wiie-ther the statement which I made was entirely accurate and was not absolutely full in every particular, and just such a statement as would have been proper for me to have made under the circumstances. Early in June, 1900, we had a written communication from the manager of the Lake Superior Power Company. This written communication followed upon a con-

versatlou which had taken place betweeu different members of the government and Mr. Olergne and between myself and Mr. Clergue in which the general policy of doing something to ensure, if possible, the construction of steel rails in our own country was very well considered. We were led to hope that so desirable an object could be attained if the company which Mr. Clergue represented could be encouraged to a sufficient extent to establish their plant by any action that the government would take. The committee will remember that we were somewhat sanguine about it, and we were led to incorporate in the Subsidy Bill of last year a clause which provided that if steel rails were manufactured in Canada and could be produced at a price and of a quality which would compare favourably with the price and quality of rails that were to be obtained elsewhere we would insist that the railway companies that we were proposing to subsidize should obtain their rails within the Dominion. I think that suggestion, when it was first mentioned to the House, met with general approval. There were one or two discordant voices, it is true, but that proposition met with general approval, and I would assume, that, having regard to the enormous expenditure which takes place in Canada year after year, the enormous outlay which is made by railway companies and by the governments for the purchase of steel rails outside of Canada, we would consider it a very desirable object indeed and one which we would be justified in making some sacrifices to accomplish if it were possible to accomplish it on business terms. This may not be present in the minds of hon. gentlemen, but 1 think X am speaking safely within bounds when I say that half of the iron import into Canada is in the form of steel rails and this will continue to increase and grow from year to year. We felt that we could not adopt a wiser policy, that we could not pursue a course which would be more promotive of the well-being of the Dominion, or tend to the establishment of a greater and more beneficial industry than this industry that we had in our minds. On .Tune 8th we received a written proposition from Mi-. Clergue and the subject was discussed in council and otherwise, discussed with Mi-. Clergue and discussed with various members of the government to see if we could arrive at anything like a satisfactory understanding with him upon such terms as would be just and fall- in the public interest. and which, at the same time, would lead to the establishment of this industry in Canada. These discussions continued from time to time. We had letters from him on various dates and we had verbal communications with him at various dates. In the month of August, as you will see later on when I read the document that 1 hold in my hand, we came to a very well-Mr. BLAIR.
understood agreement with him. Although the order was not distinctly formulated at that time, in August, we determined in council that we would give Mr. Clergue the encouragement we had decided upon, and upon which he was prepared to embark in this enterprise. I have in my hand a copy of an order in council which passed on the 9th of October and which I will read to the committee. Hon. gentlemen will note, when I read this order, that it has reference to a report, or a memorandum, which was placed by me before council on the 26th of September, which report, or memorandum, had reference to a conclusion that was arrived at by council in the month of August.
X will read the order as it passed council :
(Copy No. 89970.)
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS (Hon. A. G. Blair).

speechtext:
Extract from a report of the Committee of the hon. the Privy Council, approved by His Excellency on the 9th October, 1900.
On a memorandum dated 26th September, 1900, from the Minister of Railways and Canals, representing that under date the 8th June, 1900, the Lake Superior Power Company submitted a proposal in connection with a project of great importance, and one affecting the interests of Canada in a direction so far undeveloped, namely, the establishment of an extensive rolling mill plant adjacent to their hydraulic power at Sault Ste. Marie.
The minister states that the company represented that as the result of their mining and drilling operations on the Canadian side of Lake Superior, they had established the existence of many millions of tons of high grade Bessemer ore; that they had constructed a railway to bring this ore from tho mines to the lake, and had brought out a fleet of large ore-carrying ships, and were in readiness to commence, immediately, the erection of a steel plant for the production of rails, plate and bridge material, on the most modern principles, and on a scale of magnitude equal to any similar manufactories. In order, however, to justify the great cost which such works would entail, the company desired to obtain the assurance, to some extent, of a market before proceeding to incur further expenditure, and they submitted a proposal that the government should give them a contract for the supply to the government i ail ways of 50,000 tons of steel rails in the year 1901, and 25,000 tons annually for four years thereafter.
The minister further states that owing to the pressure of other matters and his own absence from Canada, he has been unable to bring this proposition formally before Your Excellency in Council until now. It was, however, discussed informally by the council towards the close of August, 1900, being favourably considered, and it was understood that a recommendation wrould be made and submitted by the Minister of Railways and Canals on the basis of a contract for 25,000 tons to be supplied in 1901, at $32.60 a ton (the price then being paid by the Department of Railways and Canals under its rail contract for the current year), and for a similar quantity for the five years following.
The minister, recognizing the benefits which the creation of an industry of such extent and

importance in Canada would necessarily bring directly, in the employment of labour, the expansion of mining operations and the transportation of crude materials and finished products, and indirectly, in the development of numerous other industries by which this would be served

considers that the project is one which should receive all encouragement at the hands of the government, and he recommends that authority be given for entry into an agreement with the company for the supply to the government railways of 25,000 tons (2,240 pounds to the ton) of first quality steel rails of eighty pounds to the yard, and of section prescribed by the Department of Railways and Canals, such supply to commence in the month of June, 1901, and to be completed in the month of September following; delivery to be made either at Levis or at Montreal (c.i.f), as the department may direct, and so far as practicable, in equal quantities monthly ; the price to be paid for j the said rails so delivered to be fixed, as agreed upon, at $32.60 per ton, which, as above stated, is the price now being paid by the Department of Railways and Canals.
The minister further recommends that he be authorized to contract yearly hereafter for the supply of a similar quantity of such rails during each succeeding year, for a term of five years, to be delivered either at Halifax, Port Mulgrave, Levis or St. John, as may be required by the Department of Railways and Canals, the price for the said rails to be the price for the same quality of rails in the open market in Great Britain at the time when the order therefor is given by the Department of Railways and Canals.
The committee submit the same for Your Excellency's approval.
(Sgd.) J. J. McGEE,
Clerk of the Privy Council.
Now, the committee will observe that the recommendation to council was not a recommendation to enter into a five years' contract, but it was a recommendation to enter into a contract for one year, and to be followed according to the order by subsequent contracts year by year as the years would come around. The reason that this order was presented in that way was twofold ; in the first place the government did not desire to make it. They doubted the propriety of our passing an order in council for a contract for five years ; and, moreover, the objection or difficulty was pointed out to Mr. Clergue, and Mr. Clergue, to the knowledge of the members of the council, was willing that so far as the succeeding years were concerned, the understanding should exist that the government would make these contracts year by year, and that he did not require a contract, or would not expect that a contract, would be entered into more than for the term of one year.	It was with that clear
in my mind that I made the statement to the committee, that we had only contracted explicitly for one year and had not made any permanent or fixed arrangement for the following years, further than to have an understanding with him that we would do so, and he was content to accept the order in council as being a sufficient assurance that if everything was all right he would get his contract year by year, as the time would arrive, and upon the basis and terms which were mentioned here. Well, when the matter came up the other day, I was under the impression clearly and strongly that that was the nature of the contract. I thought in my own mind that the contract had been made, and t believed that it was of that nature, and I confess that when the contract, or the draft of the proposed contract, was read here, It was a surprise to me, because it was an express and clear contract for a term of five years. But the difficulty about that contract was this ; That it had never been executed and has not been executed to this day, and never came under my observation. My deputy thought the contract was made; I supposed in the course of the numerous documents presented to me that I had executed it. I did not suppose that it would have laid over all this time, but it happened to be drawn by the law officers of the department, was sent to Mr. Clergue. and it had not been returned by Mr. Clergue at the time the question came up the other day. So that when the document was handed in the following day by the deputy minister, I think gentlemen who had it in their hands observed it was an unsigned document, and the deputy minister made a memorandum on the statement to the effect that the agreement as drawn up was drawn up in this way, and that he found it was sent to the company, but he found it had not yet been returned by the company duly executed, and he had wired that it should be done. Now, the contract as it happened had never passed under my observation. I do not know that if it had been submitted to me for signature that I would have scrutinized it closely enough to have discovered the difference between the authority which the order in council gave us and what the contract proposed to do. It might have escaped my notice or I might have carefully read it ; perhaps I would have carefully read it. At all events it did not come under my observation, and it was not read and it has not been executed, and down to this moment it has not been executed. I am quite prepared to say that Mr. Clergue will be prepared to execute the contract-I have no doubt at all upon that point-will be prepared to execute the contract when I have had an opportunity of looking into it and preparing it in accordance with the order in council which authorized me to make a contract of this limited character. I have no doubt that so far as is in Mr. Clergue's power, he will be prepared to carry out the understanding that has been arrived at and the arrangement as we have detailed it here in our order in council. It' I had a fear or a doubt I would tell the committee frankly now, that possibly Mr. Clergue may not find-though he is quite confident even to

this moment lie would be able to do so-be may not find it practicable to get his plant into sufficient working shape in order to deliver the rails this year at the time agreed upon. I hope that he may not encounter any difficulty of that kind. He is quite sure, as he writes me, that he will have no difficulty of that kind. He says his buildings are pretty well up, and his plant is all ready to install, ibut that I apprehend will be a matter that will give our friends opposite no great pain, because they seem to be very much disposed to criticise the arrangement adversely. Now, one word and I will leave this branch of the subject. The committee will see, therefore, that the order in council which I had prepared myself, and which expressed my own intention in the matter, and which expressed the intention agreed upon by my colleagues, and which expressed the conclusion of the council after the matter bad been submitted to them ; that order contained an authority to enter into an explicit contract for one year and for one year only. It contemplates that which Mr. Clergue was well satisfied with : The understanding that we would year by year enter into a new contract with him for 25,000 tons per year at a price that should be fixed according to the terms of this order. The committee, I am sure, will recognize that when endeavouring to state the matter as fully as I did to the committee the other day, I stated it with absolute accuracy, as the order will show.
Has the report and the order in council passed upon it been laid upon the Table of the House ?
I do not know that they have.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I remember seeing the contract.
The proposed contract has been handed to ' Hansard ' and this will be handed to * Hansard ' or put upon the Table of the House if desired.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I remember seeing the contract. The copy laid on the Table seems to have been mislaid-I am informed that the hon. gentleman for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) lias it.

The hon. gentleman from Lanark had it, and I got it from him and have it here in my hands now. I will let the hon. gentleman have it. I will also forward, if he desires to look at it, a copy of the order in council. The order finally passed I think on the 9th of October. I did not happen to be present at the meeting of council at which the order finallv passed, having left Ottawa on the 7th. After the Mr. BLAIR.
order did pass, a copy of it was sent on the 12th of October by the department to Mr. Clergue. From that day until I saw it after this debate commenced, I had not seen even the proposed contract; so that any error that I may have made with regard to tlie contract having been actually executed was participated in by my deputy minister, and was the result of our impressions that as a matter of course it would have been put through, whereas in the multiplicity of matters it had not been, and has not got through yet.
Now, some criticisms have been passed upon this arrangement. It has been complained of upon various grounds. I see that the newspaper press has taken up the matter, and has endorsed the attitude of some lion, gentlemen opposite. Some of their criticisms have been based on the fact that it was an agreement for five years. Nearly all, I regret to say, for their own sakes, have based their criticisms upon the assumption that we were paying or agreeing to pay $32.(50 per ton for each of the 25,000 tons, we were getting. Of course, gentlemen here know that even the draft as it was proposed by the department, and as it was sent to Mr. Clergue, contained no such engagement. What we undertook to do was to pay the price which ruled in the market of all markets to which we could properly look for a guide as to the correct value of the rails. .Tust before the House separated the other night, my hon. friend pointed to the fact that the quotations in the United States market in November were away below the price we agreed to pay. I nin not going to find fault with the statement that the prices charged by the rail makers of the United States were lower than the price we paid at that time. I am quite willing to acknowledge that that statement was correct; I deny, however, in toto the relevancy of the statement. I deny that it has any bearing in the remotest particular upon this question. We could not have induced any company to start an enterprise for the construction of steel rails in Canada if they were liable to be met by the cut prices of the combine in the United States. Why, Sir, we know that one great complaint that has been made throughout Canada, one of the foundation planks upon which our hon. friends opposite have been for years past standing, is that the effect of United States competition, when it was not opposed by a high tariff on this side, has been to enable manufacturers there to make a slaughter market of Canada; and the combine in the United States would not hesitate to offer their surplus product of rails at any price which they felt would destroy a similar manufactory in Canada. The quantity of rails they would sell in Canada in proportion to their whole output would be so small that they would not hesitate to do that, as manufacturers were in the habit of doing in times

further consideration-for at first naturally we expect them to look critically at every thing done, and even to be hypercritical if they will-when they come to understand the transaction in all its bearings, to acknowledge that the policy we have adopted is a wise one, and the transaction one that commends itself to their approval.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I really am rather surprised that the hon. gentleman should want to know what all this clamour is about. He came down on the 9tli April and told us he had entered into a certain contract. There was no story, no statement then to the House, that the contract had not been duly executed with this company. He told us what the terms of the contract were ; and from first to last there was not a word to show that the contract was not a valid and binding one, drawn up and executed by the Crown and by this company. He was asked to lay it on the Table. The next day he came down and laid the document on the Table, and told the House that that was the contract which had been executed by the Crown and the company.
I beg my hon. friend's pardon. He will not find that I made any such statement. I had no opportunity of making a statement.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman deny that every one in this House was given to understand that that paper laid on the Table contained the terms of the agreement ?
I thought it did myself.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does he deny that it was discussed for two hours in this House from that standpoint, and that the hon. gentleman never raised a single question as to its being the exact contract entered into by the Crown and this company. Then the hon. gentleman comes down and gives us three-quarters of an hour speech-a good deal of it in a very loud tone of voice-and wants to know why the time of the House has been wasted over this thing. I must confess that the hon. gentleman hardly seems to realize the position in which he is. He came down and told us there was a contract, he was asked to lay it on the Table, and did so, and then a considerable portion of the time of the House was taken up in discussing and criticising that contract. But ten days later the hon. gentleman comes down and tells us that that is not the contract at all, and wants to know what all this clamour is about, and seems to sit down quite proud of himself too-turns around to his followers and invites their applause, which they generously bestow. I do not think that the hon. gentleman was ever under greater

obligation to his followers than he has been to-day. I would like to know now whether we have really got the right contract at present. Is he quite sure that we have the exact facts ? Are we justified in going on and discussing the proposition he makes, or had we better withhold any criticism until he takes a week or ten days more to come down and enlighten us further ? I did propose to make a few remarks upon this subject, but really I feel some diffidence. I do not know whether it is worth while to discuss it further this afternoon, or whether it is not better to give the hon. gentleman a little further time in order that the House may be in a better position to adequately discuss this matter. But I suppose that he is in a position to-day to tell us exactly what the terms of the proposed contract with Mr. Clergue's company are to be. I suppose he will not deny that the House is entitled to that information, and up to the present I have not heard the hon. gentleman make it clear in what respect, if any, the contract which lie proposes to enter into with Mr. Clergue differs from that laid on the Table. If it differs from the contract laid upon the Table of the House in any important respect, I think it would be only fair for the hon. gentleman, before we discuss this matter further, to state in what respect he proposes to change the terms of that contract.

I thought I had made it perfectly clear to the committee, and I am inclined to suspect that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) is the only one who is in doubt about it. Reading the order in council, the hon. gentleman must have seen what the terms and conditions of the contract were to be. The terms were that the Lake Superior Power Company were to manufacture in Canada, at their works in Sault Ste. Marie, steel rails, 80 pounds to the yard, of a standard that should be prescribed by us, and of a certain quality, and to deliver them in Montreal or Levis in the year 1901, at a price of $32.60 per ton. The hon. gentleman must have further read that later, year after year, Mr. Clergue was entitled, as a matter of fair understanding, and as it were an engagement from the government, to come to us and say that he was prepared to enter into a new arrangement for the following year-until the five-year term had expired-to furnish us with 25,000 tons of rails of standard quality, at the price current in London; that would be an arrangement which he might reasonably expect us to make with him on the strength of that order in council.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is the only contract that the order in council would authorize us to make -a contract for one year. I explained to the committee that this contract as proposed had not passed under my own observation. After the order in council had passed, the proposed contract was sent by the department to Mr. Clergue ; and 1 had not the contract under my eye until after it had been read by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. Perhaps hon. gentlemen opposite may imagine that it is the duty of the minister personally to inspect every document that is drawn up and to be personally familiar with every transaction that takes place in the department. If that is their expectation, I can only say that parliament must get more than one human brain of my capacity to be able to compass so large an undertaking. The proposed contract was sent, in the ordinary way, by the officers of the department to Mr. Clergue. It had never come back to me for signature, and I had never seen it ; and I have no hesitation in saying that a contract drawn for five years is not such a contract as I would have knowingly executed, and not such a contract as we propose to execute, because we had no authority under the order in council to make such a contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
No one supposes that every little contract that is entered into by the Department of Railways and Canals on behalf of the Crown would necessarily be personally superintended by the minister. But. when you have a contract of this kind, purporting to involve the Crown in a liability of about $4,000,000, one would suppose that the Minister of Railways and Canals might possibly find time to glance over it. As a matter of fact, at the present time, it is very questionable whether or not Mr. Clergue cannot enforce this contract against the Crown, in view of the memorandum I see in the document laid on the Table. I see a memorandum signed by the deputy minister which says :
This agreement is drawn up on the basis of the arrangement agreed upon with Mr. Clergue on account of the company, but I find it has not yet been returned by the company duly executed, but I have wired Mr. Clergue to return the contract signed by the company.
This is dated 10th of April, 1901. So, it appears that this contract, in the terms in,
which it has been laid upon the Table, has been drawn up on the basis of an arrangement made with Mr. Clergue on account of his company, and it has not been returned by the company, duly executed, but he has been asked by telegram to return the contract signed by the company. We have not yet had the information which will be afforded by a perusal of Mr. Clergue's proposition to the government. The hon. gentleman has referred to that, and I think we are entitled to have it laid on the Table in view of that fact; find I presume the hon. gentleman has no objection to laying it on the Table ; and I should be glad if he would do so before this item passes.
Now, coming down to the merits of the arrangement which the hon. gentleman has made, I would like, in the first place, to be informed upon one point. The hon. minister has made a strong appeal to his followers in this House, on the basis of protection to Canadian industries, which appeal, I am glad to say, enlisted the sympathy of a great many of them, judging by the applause they gave him. I am happy to say that, apparently, those who had free trade views are getting rapidly cured of them when ever the exigencies of the situation seem to demand it. As touching the question of protection to Canadian manufactures, how does Mr. Clergue propose to manufacture in Canada the rails which lie is to deliver to the hon. minister this year ? I think the House is entitled to that information, because the hon. gentleman has put it forward as a strong point.
I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon, but I did not catch his question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman was engaged in something else. I will repeat the question-I suppose it is not of much importance from the hon. gentleman's standpoint : How is Mr. Clergue to manufacture in Canada the rails which he is to deliver this year ? Has he works, or will he have works capable of furnishing 25,000 tons of rails within the time specified by the proposed contract ?

I suppose that Mr. Clergue, having engaged to deliver the rails, will have the means of manufacturing them, and will produce them as other manufacturers do. I presume he will have the necessary plant for that purpose. It was, I believe, confidently anticipated by him, as it was by us, that there would be time, ample time, from the date when this understanding was arrived at, for Mr. Clergue to put up the necessary buildings and provide the necessary plant. I confess I do not see the drift of the hon. gentleman's inquiry ; for I think it must be presumed that Mr. Clergue would expect to establish a plant and get j his ore and produce his rails precisely the

same as other manufacturers produce theirs. And the rails have to he manufactured in Canada.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentle man has made this so intensely clear that it is hardly worth while perhaps for anything further to be said on the subject. I put the question to the hon. gentleman for this reason : I understood he was in a hurry to make a contract for these rails last autumn because he would require them this summer. He says it is necessary to order the rails nine or ten months in advance. It being absolutely necessary that he should have these rails this summer, he was absolutely obliged to make this contract in the month of November last with Mr. Clergue. That is the position the hon. gentleman has placed before the committee. That is a plain and reasonable position. Then the hon. gentleman put forward another perfectly plain and reasonable position, namely, that he made this contract with Mr. Clergue for one year-not for five years- but for one year, for the purpose 0f encouraging Canadian industries. Now I notice in passing that this contract does not in express terms provide that these rails shall be manufactured in Canada at all. It does recite something with respect to the protection and encouragement of Canadian industries ; but when you come to the operative part of this proposed contract you do not find a single word about Mr. Clergue manufacturing these rails in Canada. Now does the hon. gentleman desire the House to understand that he believes Mr. Clergue will be able to furnish these rails between June and September, and manufacture them in Canada ? I would like an answer from the hon. gentleman on that point.

I can tell the hon. gentlemau that in the month of August last when the arrangement was made with Mr. Clergue, and down until October, and since then, there has been every expectation on the part of the government, certainly there has been on my part, that Mr. Clergue would have his plant in shape to be able to produce these rails, and Mr. Clergue guarantees and assures me down to the present moment that he is going to be able to do it. Of course if he does not do it, we shall not have to pay for them, that is all. But what does the hon. gentleman mean ? You have no rail manufactory in Canada ; you want to encottrage the establishment of a rail manufactory in, Canada. There has not been a blow struck, there has not been a brick laid in a building, there has not been a pound of machinery installed without some inducement. Now you can enter into a contract under such circumstances as we did here, saying to the intended manufacturer : You produce for us in Canada a certain quantity of rails at such a time, and we will Mr. BLAIR.
take them from you. And he goes to work, and we expected he would go to work. 1 believe from what Mr. Clergue has said that he has gone to work. I believe that Mr. Clergue is competent, and that he can supply us with these rails. I am afraid-I have said already that I am a little doubtful that he has been too sanguine in his expectations ; I have said that two or three times already. I do not say that with the view of throwing any doubt at all upon Mr. Clergue's ability, but I fear that obstacles may prove to be more than he has anticipated, more than he has found it possible to overcome; but he says not. Now what does the hon. gentleman complain of ? If the rails do not materialize, if they are not produced, no harm has been done in any way. We have made a legitimate effort to have this thing accomplished.
The hon. gentleman says there is nothing in this contract about the rails being manufactured in Canada. I have already said that until that document was read over in the House it never passed under my eye. I would like our hon. friends opposite to take charge of the Department of Railways and Canals for a while, and see whether they are going to be able to read and study over every big contract that happens to be made in the department. We have a regular law department, and Justice Department, which looks over these matters, and when an order in council passes, instructions are given to have a contract based upon that order in council, drawn up, not by the minister, not by the deputy minister, but by the proper officer; and if the contract was drawn in defective form, and when it came to be executed by the minister he found it in that defective form, why, undoubtedly he would have it amended and put right. That has already happened in many eases, we cannot avoid these things by any possibility. The hon. gentleman says this contract says nothing about the rails being made in Canada. Well, that was the very basis of1 the arrangement, and no contract will be executed by me which does not contain that stipulation, unless, on inspection of the clauses, I find that they give every guarantee that these rails should be manufactured in Canada.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the leader of the opposition will allow me, I may say that I know personally that these works are very near completion. About two weeks ago I talked with Mr. Clergue and asked him directly the question with regard to this contract, as to when he expected to be able to start the delivery of these rails for the government, and he gave me every assurance that he would be delivering them in the first part of the month of August next. I consider that when we have an assurance of that kind from Mr. Clergue, we have every reason to believe that the contract will be carried out as we anticipate.
Does the hon. gentleman personally know whether the rolling mill has really been commenced ?
The works are all up, and the plant is almost installed.
The rolling mill plant ?
Yes, the steel rail plant.

I do not know personally anything about it, but the accounts we get in the press are entirely contrary to what the hon. gentleman has told us. Of course, if he tells me what he personally knows about it I shall accept his word. I would be very glad indeed if the information that he has given turns out to be correct. I may say that I have made some inquiries about this matter, and the information that I have obtained does not lead me to hope that the hon. gentleman's anticipations will be realized. I had some little difference of opinion with the Minister of Finance the other day as to when the proposed rolling mills of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company would be able to begin operations. I have taken pains to verify my information, and I find I was right about it. The Dominion Iron and Steel Company began to consider the construction of rolling mills early last autumn, and as far back as the month of December it was announced to the public that they proposed to engage in this manufacture of steel rails. I made inquiries, and find that the plans for their rolling mills have been in the hands of their architects since the first of this year, and further I find that notwithstanding that, they do not expect the rolling mills can be completed before the 31st of December, and further, they do not think they will probably be completed until two or three months after that, although I understand their manager says that the work will be completed by the 31st of December. Now I do not suppose that the gentlemen who are engaged in that enterprise are less capable of building rolling mills than Mr. Clergue and the gentlemen with whom he is associated. I know he is a very capable and energetic gentleman, and has command of large capital, apparently, and he can do this work as rapidly as any other man ; but the gentlemen who are interested in the enterprise to which I have referred have also these advantages, and I see no reason why they should not be able to complete works of that kind just as quickly as Mr. Clergue. Now, we are very glad indeed that the Minister of Railways and Canals and the right hon. gentleman have told us that we will not have to pay for these rails until we get them. That is one consolation : but the ground the hon. gentleman took, the reason for which he enlarged at some length upon the excellence of his proposal, was that rails were going to be manufactured this 112
year, and were going to be manufactured by this company in Canada. Now, it remains a doubtful question, according to his own statement, as to whether these rails can be manufactured in Canada this year. If they are not manufactured in Canada, is Mr. Clerge going to furnish them ?
Certainly not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Mr. Clergue is not to furnish them ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well, the contract which has been laid on the Table of the House merely provides that Mr. Clergue is to manufacture and deliver. Now that would leave it open, apparently, to Mr. Clerge, unless the operative words of this contract are controlled by the recital, to manufacture them anywhere he might see fit. I certainly do think that the hon. minister should be most grateful to the opposition for pointing out to him certain provisions of this contract in which he does not now seem to concur, because it is perfectly apparent that if the criticism which was made upon this document by the opposition some ten days ago had not been made, this document would have been executed by Mr. Clergue, it would have been returned to the government and the government would have been bound by it.
Not much.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The memorandum, on the face of this document, shows exactly the position with respect to that.
I presume that until I signed the contract it would not be binding.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: But, when the chief officer of his own department says that this agreement has been drawn up on the basis of the arrangement agreed on with Mr. Clergue, and when the document was signed and executed by Mr. Clergue, the hon. gentleman and the government might have a great deal of difficulty in getting out of it if Mr. Clergue was determined to enforce it.
It would not take you very long to show that we would not have a great deal of difficulty.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman does me too much credit. I think I would have a great deal of difficulty, and I think the hon. gentleman would have a great deal of difficulty in getting out of a situation of that kind. I was rather amused



at tlie bon. gentleman's reply to ns on this side of the House when we criticised this arrangement which he proposed to make with Mr. Clergue, particularly in view of the fact that he, himself, admits, so far as I understand, that the price of rails in the United States at least, is some $5, $6, or $7 less now than the price he proposes to pay.

No, I did not admit anything of the kind. I said that I would not deny or dispute the statement which was made by the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. S'proule) that rails had been offered, or were sold, in November last for $5, or S6, a ton less than the price we agreed to pay in England. I do not know that to be the fact, but I am not going to dispute it because it does not seem relevant.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman mean to say that the price of rails in the United States has no relation to the price of rails in England ? I understood him to make that statement in his address to the committee. I would have supposed that when steam communication is so frequent between the United States and England, there would be some connection between the price of rails in the United States and the price in England, and when the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) has shown that the price in the United States was so many dollars below the price which the hon. gentleman has agreed to pay, the price in England must have some relation to that price and make it so very much greater. Now, the only thing I have to say in conclusion, is that if there has been any time wasted in the debate upon the extraordinary proposition which the hon. gentleman has brought down to this House, if there has been any useless criticism made upon the hon. gentleman's proposition by reason of the fact that we were not discussing the contract which the hon. gentleman proposes to make, then, he and not the opposition is responsible for it. In respect to the vote which he asks from this House, I think that I am not demanding too much for this side of the House when I ask that the proposition made by Mr. Clergue should be laid on the Table of the House and that the hon. gentleman, should have the courtesy before this vote passes to lay on the Table of the House, a draft, if not the executed contract which he proposes to make with Mr. Clergue. We have had one contract which turns out to be not the contract at all. We are entitled to have a draft of the contract or the executed contract between the government and Mr. Clergue before we allow this item to pass. I would ask the hon. gentleman to say if I am requesting anything that is unreasonable ?
I think I may say that the hon.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax), is asking something that is very unreasonable. I do not propose to acknowledge that the hon. gentleman is making a usual or customary suggestion at all when he asks tliat the draft should be laid on the Table of the House before we make our contract with Mr. Clergue. We have given the committee the terms of the order in council which authorizes the Department of Railways and Canals to make a contract for the manufacture of a certain quality of steel rails in Canada at a certain price for the year 1901. I propose that the contract, when it is drawn for execution by the parties, shall be in entire accord with the terms of the order in council. It will only be a contract for this year; we cannot do anything else. I have no objection at all, however, in respect to the other hon. gentleman's suggestion that we should place upon the Table of the House a copy of Mr. Clergue's proposition. I have the original proposition in my hand and I will have a copy made and laid on the Table to-morrow if the hon. gentleman desires it as I understand he does.
I would like to ask the hon. minister whether that important telegram from his deputy to Mi-. Clergue was sent without the minister's knowledge ?
Which is that ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The one of the 10th of April asking Mr. Clergue to return the contract executed. I would like to know whether that was sent without the minister's knowledge ?

The contract, I have told the committee over and over again, which was drawn, was drawn in the usual branch of the department. It was not drawn by me. It did not happen to be submitted to me before it was sent to Mr. Clergue. The order in council was sent from council to that department in the ordinary way, and I presumed that the contract, when it was drawn, would be drawn in accordance with the order in council. Therefore, I was entirely unaware of the terms of the draft as sent to Mr. Clergue until it was read here in this House. I know that we had taken all the precautions in the recommendation which was made by council in the order which was passed to carry out the conclusions at which we had arrived, and to protect the department in every respect.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I ask the hon. gentleman to say whether the telegram, sent by his deputy on the 10th of April, the last day on which this subject was before the committee, was sent by his department without his knowledge. Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to answer ?

The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND [DOT]CANALS. I knew that the deputy minister was going to wire Mr. Clergue about the contract, but I do not think that I saw the telegram. No, I did not see the telegram. He certainly sent the telegram with my full permission and consent.

The hon. gentleman admits that it was sent by his authority. 1 could not imagine for a moment that the deputy minister would send so important a message, one involving a contract for Sl,-000,000, without consulting his chief. I am quite sure the deputy minister did consult his minister and that the minister, when he brought that paper down and laid it on the Table, knew that the contract was not executed. That was the object of my question.

When we were coming over to the House the other day from the department, as I was leaving to come, with the understanding that my estimates would be up, I said to the deputy :	Mr. Haggart
asked you to have that contract. I would like you to bring a copy of it over with you. He mentioned to me then, which was the first information I had on the subject, that the contract had not been returned by Mr. Clergue, and of course it would then follow that I had not executed it. I said to the deputy minister :	You had better put a
memorandum on the back of this paper that you bring over to show that it has not been executed and he did that. I did not even see that. I think the first time I saw it was not until after it came over here.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I think that we have now got pretty closely the facts connected with this contract. On the 9th of April, the hon. gentleman told the committee that he had entered into a contract with Mr. Clergue for the supplying of 25,000 tons of 80-pound rails. He was then asked by the Hon. Mr. Haggart to produce the contract and he promised to do so. The next day the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) brought in what was supposed to be a contract. It happens not to have been a contract at all. It was a paper containing the terms of a contract, but not executed by the government, though I take it the government was in honour bound to carry out that contract, having passed it in council.
If It was in accordance with the order.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It was not executed by Mr. Clergue, and there was a memorandum attached showing that the deputy minister on that date, April 10, had telegraphed Mr. Clergue to return the contract executed. Now, what was the position taken by the minister when he was before the committee the other day with the knowledge that that 1121
contract had not been executed? Did he tell the members of this House that there was no contract? Certainly not. He defended it as a contract. Again and again, in reply to member after member who questioned him upon it, he not only did not tell the House that there was no such contract in existence, but he defended the terms of tlie contract. In reply to the leader of the opposition, the Minister of Railways said :
Well, now, what are the terms of that contract?	[DOT]
This is the paper which was not a contract at all, according to the minister's present position.
What are the terms of that contract? If it is open to criticism, then let the hon. gentleman criticise it as it is his right to do. Do the terms state that we are to pay to this Lake Superior Power Company any price they may ask. Are we to pay a price higher than the market price ? No, we are not to pay a price higher than the market price.
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) was not referring to the first year of the contract, because there was a fixed price as to that. He was referring to the future years ; he was referring to the contract for the four following years, and yet he did not utter a word to inform this House as to the fact known to himself, but which the House did not know, that no contract had been executed. Then this follws :
This is the contract.

That is the contract, is it not?
May I ask the minister if that was candid in face of the fact that it was not a contract at all.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, certainly, that is a contract to buy for five years.

Well, I say that we had no explicit arrangement, because the price is entirely indefinite.
Not a word from the minister questioning the fact that he had entered into a contract for the delivery of 125,000 tons, only that the price was left indefinite, os we know it had been, and as it was intended to be. The minister goes on to say :
We have an understanding that we are to take from them rails providing they are willing and ready to sell them to us at the market price in England.
That, again, refers to the future years and not to the current year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: You are obliged to take them by your contract.

We are not obliged unless they agree to give them to us at the prevailing price in England. What ivas the minister speaking of then if it was not the contract ? He was speaking of the very terms of the contract for the four years, and not for the first year. The minister then referred to locomotives, and he justified his locomotive contract on the

same terms as the rail contract. Then the minister goes on to say :
If he cannot understand the question, I am not going to undertake to do it lor him. We have agreed to take these rails for the current year for these prices.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: fi. And for the succeeding four years.
We have not agreed for more than one year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is not the contract signed?

It does not fix the price at all.
*Why did not the minister tell the House then that the contract was not signed ? Every one was discussing it on the assumption that the minister had done what he said the day before he was going to do, namely, that he was going to lay on the Table of the House the contract with Mr. Clergue for 125,000 tons of rails, and the minister was discussing the question, and he saw that every gentleman on this side of the House was discussing it under the belief that there was a contract. The minister said again :
Certainly, we will take for the four years 25,000 tons yearly, but have not fixed a price. We will take the rails at the current market rate in England.
That was the position the minister assumed on the 10th of April. The hon. gentleman was not then taking the position that he had no contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do not say that now. I say that we had a fair square understanding with Mr. Clergue all the way through. He was willing, to treat that order in council as an understanding, hut we had not an explicit contract for more than one year. That is what I have been saying all along.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The minister talks about an understanding. Why, this is no understanding. This is a deliberate contract. The government undertook to buy 125,000 tons of rails, and Mr. Clergue undertakes to deliver them. The only question that was left open was the question of price for the four years. The hon. minister has considered this for ten days and he comes down now and he tells us that there was no contract at all. What is the position of the minister in that respect ? On the 9th of April lie was asked why the intention of the government to buy such an enormous quantity of rails involving nearly $4,000,000 was not placed before the House last session. The hon. minister then took the position that there was such a rush of business, it was so close to the end of the session, that they had not time to discuss these things, and that they therefore left it for a less busy season. Now, it appears that the minister took it up again in August, and again in September, and again in October, only four weeks before the general elections, and then when Mr. BARKER.
he had so much time upon his hands, so little to do, he enters into a contract involving $4,000,000, and after all that contract is one that a child would not enter into. The hon. gentleman recites in the order the intention to promote the manufacture of rails in this country, and yet throughout the whole contract there is not one word which compels the contractors to manufacture one rail in this country. Taking the best view of it in the interest of the minister, if the contractors had manufactured one-twentieth part of the rails in this country they would have complied with the contract, but there is not even one word in the operative part of the contract referring to the manufacture of the rails in this country at all. The Minister of Railways must have known that. I can hardly imagine that when the hon. minister was asked to bring that contract down here on the 9th of April that he did not look at it before it was brought into this House.
I did not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: His deputy told him it was not executed. Is it conceivable : can any business man suppose that a minister charged with the enormous interests of this Railway Department, knowing that the subject under discussion was a contract of a most unusual character, knowing that that contract had not been executed, knowing that he was telegraphing, through his deputy, to the other party to execute it, is it conceivable that the minister under such circumstances would send that message off without seeing what the contract was about? If the hon. gentleman so acted in a private capacity he would be laughed at, and yet he thinks he can turn off the responsibility upon his deputy or upon some other officer of his department. I have always understood that a minister is responsible for his department. It is the first time I ever heard of a minister attempting to shirk responsibility in this way. The truth is that when the minister brought down that paper he knew that it was not executed. But he defended it here in the House as if it had been executed. And yet he would have us believe that he took so little interest in this subject, that knowing his deputy was telegraphing to Sault Ste. Marie to have it executed, knowing how important were the terms of that contract to this country, he, although he had the countract in his hands, neglected to read it, and came to the House and defended the terms of it, without knowing what they were, although it would not have taken him five minutes to read the paper.

Let me tell the hon. gentleman one fact. Of all the hundreds of thousands of contracts'that pass through my department, I do not think there is one in a hundred that I ever see until the other party

signs it and it is submitted to me for signature. When it is so submitted, I may eall attention to some change which I think ought to be made in it, and then the contract is redrawn, and sent to be resigned. I am not going to throw any responsibility upon any one else ; I take the entire responsibility of the whole matter. The hon. gentleman misrepresented my position. At the same time, it is open to me to make an explanation to the House of what occurred- I do not care whether the hon. gentleman accepts it or not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Are we to understand that when the hon. Minister of Railways, or any other minister, comes to the House, after an afternoon's debate criticising expenditure, and when papers have been demanded and promised, it is reasonable for the minister to bring down such a paper as this, without calling attention to the nonexecution of the contract, or to that most important message, which, as the leader of the opposition says, might commit the government by its very terms? The minister does that, and says there are hundreds of thousands of such contracts which he does not see. Why, it is monstrous. If the hon. gentleman were dealing with a contract in ordinary business involving a thousand dollars instead of millions, he would not do that. We have had three versions of this affair already ; but the fourth version, the most extraordinary, is that the hon. gentleman can excuse himself by saying that he did not read the contract.

My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker), if he will permit me to say so, is generally fair in discussing matters that come before this House; but I do not think that on this occasion he treats the House with his usual fairness. Matters in this case are a little involved because of some misunderstanding on both sides. The broad question before the House is whether or not the government have done right in taking authority to enter into a contract with a Canadian company for the manufacture of Canadian rails. This question has been somewhat entangled with other questions. My hon. friend has rather rebuked us for not having taken authority last session to enter into a contract with the Lake Superior Power Company. But the matter was not contemplated at that time. No one in the month of July last thought it would be possible within the year 1901 to have steel rails manufactured in Canada ; but it happens that we have been so fortunate as to see this day dawning upon us. This country has been a large constructor of railways up to the present time, but our misfortune has been that up to the present time we have not been able to supply our own railways with Canadian rails, but have had to import them from abroad. I have seen enough of this discussion, and the temper of the House
on both sides and the temper of the press, to be satisfied that hon. gentlemen opposite approve of the idea and the conduct of the government in the main, though they may not perhaps approve of every detail of the transaction ; that is to say, they approve of the action of the government if it leads to the construction of steel rails in Canada henceforth, as we hope it will. Now, in the month of August last we entered into negotiations with Mr. Clergue, the manager of the Lake Superior Power Company, for the manufacture of these rails. Negotiations of that character are not concluded in a day. It took some time to complete them, and in the month of September following, the Minister of Railways brought to council a recommendation to enter into a contract which would secure the manufacture of steel rails in Canada. After a preamble, the minister's recommendation reads thus :
The undersigned has the honour to represent that under date the 8th June, 1900, the Lake Superior Power Company submitted to him a proposal in connection with a project of great importance, and one affecting the interests of Canada in a direction so far undeveloped, namely, the establishment of an extensive rolling mill plant adjacent to their hydraulic power at Sault Ste. Marie.
That the company represented that as the result of their mining and drilling operations on the Canadian side of Lake Superior, they established the existence of many millions of tons of high grade Bessemer ore; that they had constructed a railway to bring this ore from the mines to the lake, and had brought out a fieet of large cre-carrying ships, and were in readiness to commence, Immediately, the erection of a steel plant for the production of rails, plate and bridge materials on the most modern principles, and on a scale of magnitude equal to any similar manufactories. In order, however, to justify the great cost which such works would entail, the company desired to obtain the assurance, to some extent, of a market before proceeding to incur further expenditure, and they submitted a proposal that the government should give them a contract for the supply to the government railways of 50,000 tons of steel rails in the year 1901, and 25,000 tons annually for four years thereafter.
That owing to the pressure of other matters, and his cwn absence from Canada, the undersigned has been unable to bring this proposition formally before Your Excellency in Council until now. It was, however, discussed informally by the cabinet towards the close of August, 1900, being favourably considered, and it was understood that a recommendation would be made and be submitted by the Minister of Railways and Canals on the basis of a contract for 25,000 tons to be supplied in 1901 at $32.60 a ton (the price then being paid by the Department of Railways and Canals under its rail contract for the current year) and for a similar quantity for the five years following.
The undersigned, recognizing the benefits which the creation of an industry of such extent and importance in Canada would necessarily bring directly, in the employment of labour, the expansion of mining operations and the transportation of crude materials and finished products, and indirectly, in the development of

numerous other industries by which this vould be served-considers that the project is one which should receive all encouragement at the hands of the government, and he recommends that authority be given for entry into an agree*-ment with the company for the supply to the government railways of 25,000 tons (2,240 pounds to the ton) of first quality steel rails of eighty pounds to the yard, and of section prescribed by the Department of Railways and Canals, such supply to commence in the month of June, 1901, and to be completed in the month of September following; delivery to be made either at Levis or at Montreal (c-i.f), as the department may direct, and so far as practicable, in equal quantities, monthly; the price to be paid for the said rails so delivered to be fixed, as agreed upon, at $32.60 per ton, which, as above stated, is the price now Deing paid by the Department of Railways and Canals.
The undersigned further recommends that he be authorized to contract yearly hereafter, for the supply of a similar quantity of such rails during each succeeding year, for a term of five years, to be delivered either at Halifax, Port Mulgrave or St. John, as may be required by the Department of Railways and Canals, the price for the said rails to be I he price for the same quantity of rails in the open market in Great Britain at the time when the order therefor is given by the Department of Railways and Canals:
This proposition was then considered by council, and on the 9th of October the council authorized the Minister of Railways to enter into such a contract. A contract was drawn up by the legal adviser of the department, and sent to Mr. Clergue for execution. The minister then left the further details and the execution of the contract to be carried out by the officers of his department. He frankly tells us to-day that he was under a misapprehension when he brought the matter to the attention of the House, supposing that the contract had been .'executed ; for it turns out now that the contract was not executed. My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is not exactly fair to the Minister of Railways when he said that the minister had been disingen-ious when he stated on the 10th of April that the contract had been executed, whereas, in point of fact, it had not. What I would observe is that the minister was under the impression at that moment that the contract had been executed, but that he subsequently discovered that it had been sent over to Mr. Clergue for his signature before the minister had been called on to sign it. Had the contract been previously brought to the minister to sign, he would have seen that it was not in accordance with the order in council. The discrepancy between the draft of contract and the order in council is this.

If the right hon. gentleman will allow me to interrupt him, my point is this-that on the 10th of April, when the minister laid that contract or paper on the Table, he knew then that it had not been executed, and yet his whole argument in this House was in defence of Sir WILFRID LATJRIER.
that contract, and he did not tell us that it had never been executed.

My hon. friend must realize that the minister, when he went to the department, found that the draft contract had been sent to Mr. Clergue. The following day, when he came to discuss the matter, he naturally assumed that the contract had been drawn exactly as authorized by the order in council. But, later he found that the contract was not in full accordance with the order in council, and the discrepancy between the two is this. The draft contract, which has been laid on the Table, is a contract for five years, whereas the order in council only authorized the minister to enter into a contract for one year, at $32.60 per ton. But, thereafter, he is authorized to enter each year into a subsequent contract, at the prices then ruling in England, during a term of four years. But the contract has to be renewed from year to year, and there can be only one contract for each year. The contract is not a binding one for five years, as is mentioned in the draft. That point is very clear. The only thing binding upon the government is the order in council and nothing else, and that order in council only authorizes the minister to enter into a contract for one year, but authorizes him to make a new contract each succeeding year during four years, and the prices are to be those ruling on the English market at each renewal.
My hon. friend said that the government would be bound in honour to carry out the contract signed and executed by Mr. Clergue. I need not say to my hon. friend that the government is bound, not only in honour, but legally, to carry out such a contract as is framed according to the order in council and no other. If in any way the contract varies from the terms of the order in council, it would not be binding on the government. But, all this quibbling is simply a little surplusage of no consequence to the issue. The question is simply whether or not the government acted wisely in the arrangement it came to with the Lake Superior Power Company last October.
What other point has been raised ? It has been said that the government entered into a contract without authority. Nothing of the kind. We had the authority, because in the Supply Bill voted last year, there is an appropriation for steel rails.
The point has also been made that we have entered into a contract for five years. If we had, the point might be well taken, that we had overstepped our authority. But, we did nothing of the kind. We made a contract for one year only, but the minister was authorized afterwards to enter into another contract each succeeding year for four years, but he could not do so unless parliament voted him the money to carry it out. So that, we have not assumed to bind parliament for five years, but simply

for one year, but we have anticipated that parliament would readily support the policy of giving our contracts for the steel rails we require to that company, which is able to supply us with steel rails manufactured in Canada, instead of the foreign rails which we have been purchasing hitherto.
Then, the question is, whether in this contract for one year, we are paying too dear for the rails. The price agreed on for that year is $32.60, and the prices to be agreed on for the coming years are to be those ruling in the English market, and to that,
I presume, there can be no objection. The only contention that can arise, therefore, at this moment is, whether the price we are ' paying this year is too high or not. What are the facts ? The facts are that at the time we made the contract the ruling price in England was $32.60, and had the delivery been made at that moment there could not have been a word said against the price. But, since then, we are told that it has gone down. Possibly it has. But you have to make your contracts in advance and agree on a price, and both purchaser and seller have to take their chances on the market fluctuations'. Instead of the price going down, it has gone up ; but, had the reverse happened, Mr. Clergue would have been the loser instead of us. Had we agreed to a fixed price of $32.60 for a term of five years, there might be some ground for criticism, but the contract is only for one year. Moreover, even if the price has gone down to $26 per ton, if I am correctly informed, the day before yesterday the price in New York rose to $28 per ton, showing the fluctuations of the market, and under the circumstances, even if we are to pay a little more this year than the actual market rate, I think the Canadian parliament and people will support us in the policy we have adopted of having our rails supplied by a Canadian company.

Just one observation in reply to the right hon. gentleman.
I understood him to say that there was no intention to bind parliament for more than one year by the terms of the order in council ?
I gave the terms of the order in council.

In the order in council this is laid down :
They submitted a proposal that the government should give them a contract for the supply to the government railways of 50,000 tons of steel rails in the year 1901 and 25,000 tons annually for four years thereafter.
Further on in the recital I find :
It was understood that a recommendation would be made and submitted by the Minister of Railways and Canals on the basis of a contract for 25,000 tons to be supplied in 1901 at $32.60 a ton (the price then being paid by the Department of Railways and Canals under its 1
rail contract for the current year) and for a similar quantity for the five years following.
What is this but a contract for 25,000 tons to be supplied in 1901, at $32.60, and a similar quantity for the five years following? The hon. gentleman does not find a proposal to bind parliament for only one year in that language. And, when he comes to the operative part of it, what does he find? After providing that there should be a contract for 25,000 tons, at $32.60 per ton for 1901, what follows?
The minister further recommends that be be authorized to contract yearly hereafter for the supply of a similar quantity of such rails during *each succeeding year for the term of five years. And the minister, under that language, irrespective of council, irrespective of parliament, can go out and make a contract for five years, binding upon the government.
If he can get the appropriation.
He may contract year by year.

If he gets the appropriation. I am astonished to hear such language from the Minister of Finance. Does not he know that under the usage of parliament and government in England such a contract would be binding upon the government, and that any government that undertook to depart from a contract made with such authority would be different from any government existing in any British country ? If he knows anything of the history of parliamentary government in England, one instance will at once occur to his mind where a contract covering several years was made by a government just going out of power, and, thougli it was a bad contract, it was carefully observed by the government succeeding. And, so' far as this government is concerned, which, according to the hon. gentleman, is to be in power for twenty-five years, do I understand from the right hon. the Prime Minister or the Minister of Finance, that, though there is authority here to make the contract for five years, they would be prepared to repudiate it ?
No, but my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) will see that, the Minister of Railways being authorized to contract yearly, the terms are to be revised yearly by parliament.

The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is not stating the terms of this order in council according to the language of it

The minister further recommends that he be authorized to contract yearly hereafter for the supply of a similar quantity of such rails during each succeeding year for the term of live years. He can make that contract without going back to council, and any government will i be bound to ask parliament for the appro-

priation and be bound to go out of power if parliament does not grant it. And tbe right hon. gentleman knows it as well as I know it, having the acquaintance that we all know he has with the usages of parliamentary government in this country. It is useless for the hon. gentleman to pretend that this order in council does not bind this country for five years, the terms of it having been communicated to Mr. Clergue. As long as
Well, what is the matter
Does the hon. Minister of Finance desire to ask any question ?	*
What is wrong with the transaction, even if that Ss correct ?

I want the transaction to be understood by the House. We heard a statement by the hon. gentleman's leader that this was not a contract binding the government for five years, and I am simply trying to make It plain that the hon. gentleman's leader does not truly apprehend the terms of the order in council when he makes that statement. That is my answer to the Minister of Finance. I think the statement of the right hon. gentleman who leads the House was not very accurate, but I think it was very much more pertinent than the suggestion of the Minister of Finance that the government could get out of the arrangement entered into under this order in council by declining to ask parliament for the necessary appropriation.
The suggestion of the hon. gentleman-or, is he finished ? I do not wish to interrupt him.

No, I had not finished. I would like to inquire of the Minister of Railways and Canals with regard to this telegram which has been referred to by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). The Minister of Railways and Canals says he sent a telegram to Mr. Clergue on the 10th of April-or, rather, he instructed his deputy to send a telegram- and we know what the instructions were from the memorandum appearing on the back of the document laid on the Table of the House.
The hon. gentleman can judge from that memorandum what the telegram was, but he cannot say I gave instructions, because I did not give instructions.
speakername: Tiie MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to say that he instructed his deputy to send a telegram to Mr. Clergue to have the contract executed and returned. If I am in error he will kindly correct me, because I do not wish to misrepre-

sent him. I understood that this took place after the matter was discussed in this House. If the hon. gentleman will correct me at once if I am making any mistake, I shall be glad, because I desire to be entirely accurate. Well, if that is the case, it seems to me that the hon. gentleman's contention this afternoon that he had never seen this contract does not amount to much, because it appears, if I understand the facts rightly, that after this contract had been criticised and discussed in this House and
No, no.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Then I am not correct in the assertion that I have just made, and to which I understood the hon. gentleman to assent, that he had sent the telegram after the discussion in this House.
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: After the first ^discussion ?

No, the hon. gentleman misunderstands me. What occurred was this : There was a promise made by me, at the instance of the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. ITaggart), that I would bring down the contract. I asked the deputy minister to make a note, so that we could bring the contract when we next came. When we came, the deputy minister brought over the contract with him, but when I met him, shortly before coming to the House, he informed me that the contract had not been executed by Mr. Clergue. That was just before we came over. That was before the discussion took place in the House. I said : You had better telegraph Mr. Clergue upon the subject.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I at once accept the hon. gentleman's statement, but I do not think it puts him in any better position ?
I do not care whether it does or not. I was simply answering the hon. gentleman's question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well, I hope the hon. gentleman will not lose his temper over this discussion

I am not losing my temper. But the hon. gentleman would imply that I was resenting his statement, and so would convey the impression that 1 was endeavouring to put the case in a more favourable light. What I was doing was answering the hon. gentleman's statement, which was not correct.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If I have stated anything to offend the hon. gentleman, I am very sorry

I -would not offend the hon. gentleman for the world.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax)-or if I have said anything to put the hon. gentleman out of humour. But perhaps he will he good enough to give me his attention for a minute or two. This subject was discussed on the 10th. He sent the telegram to Mr. Clergue the same day, asking him to execute the contract
