speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It was sent by my deputy.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well, we will be entirely exact-it was sent by the hon. gentleman's deputy, by the hon. gentleman's instruction, and the hon. gentleman had nothing more to do with it. Now, the subject was pretty thoroughly discussed in this House on the 10th, but, did the hon. gentleman send any telegram to Mr. Clergue not to execute the contract, as it was not in accordance with the order in council ?
When I ascertained that it was not executed, I instructed the deputy minister to notify Mr. Clergue.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman does not quite apprehend my question. On the 10th, he telegraphed to Mr. Clergue to execute this contract. On the same day, the terms of it were discussed and criticised in this House, and the hon. gentleman must have become aware then that its terms were not in accordance with the order in council, for he tells us that now. Did the hon. gentleman, on the 10th, send a telegram to Mr. Clergue countermanding the instructions to execute the contract ?

The deputy minister tells me that when the proposed contract came to be read in the House, I instructed him to wire to Mr. Clergue on the subject, and he wired- to Mr. Clergue, stating, it appears, that the minister had never seen this draft contract and he wished it immediately returned unexecuted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I suppose the hon. minister will have no objection to laying the telegraphic correspondence upon the Table. I shall be glad if he will do so. Now, I think it is abundantly clear from the terms of this contract that the Minister of Railways and Canals has received from the council authority to make an agreement covering five years. The terms of the order in council would authorize an agreement at once for five years, but whether it authorizes that or not, it does authorize the minister to make a contract without going back to parliament and council.
Without going back to council.

But the right hon. gentleman said that so far as parliament is concerned, the minister had no authority beyond a year. So I understand the right hon. gentleman's remark with regard to the appropriation. If the minister, under the authority of an order in council, made a bargain for five years, how could parliament refuse an appropriation ? How could any government refuse to ask parliament for an appropriation ? That is the point in respect of which I think the hon. gentleman's observations to the House were not quite relevant.

My hon. friend will agree that there is a difference between making a contract for five years, or authorizing a minister to make a contract for five years, and authorizing a minister to make a contract yearly for five years. The difference in point of fact is not considerable, because parliament has power to revise the price every year. That is an advantage which the government possesses under this contract. Parliament is bound to ratify the contract or to reject it. If they ratify it, then parliament divests itself of its annual supervision over the terms of this contract. The yearly supervision of parliament is maintained over this contract, because year after year the minister makes a contract, not for five years, not for four years, not for three years, but for one year at a time, and the terms of this contract are submitted to parliament each year. My hon. friend will agree that there is a difference, if there is no difference then language has no meaning.

The point between us is not very great, but I think it is entirely clear. In regard to prices, the price is on the same basis always, to be determined by the current price in England. Therefore, there is no distinction so far as that is concerned. The hon. gentleman's distinction founded upon any suggestion of yearly revision by parliament is wrong. If the hon. gentleman contended that this contract should not toe made without coming to parliament yearly, I would be content. The point I made is that the minister, under this order in council, can make this contract in any year without coming to parliament, and without going to council. When he has made that contract parliament is bound to vote an appropriation, the government of which he is a member is bound to ask par-lament for that appropriation.
The minister may make a contract every year without the authorization of parliament, but he has every time to come to parliament to get the sanction of that contract.

The Prime Minister has told the House that the issue before the country is purely one of dollars and cents. I say that the issue is one as to the method

of doing business. This debate shows we have an incompetent minister in this respect, we have an incompetent law department, and we have a leader of the government who permits this incompetent way of doing business to go on, and this incompetent minister to be a member of his administration. The Liberals, not only in this parliament, but when in opposition, have advocated the doctrine of governmental responsibility in protecting the public interest. But they are not here for that purpose at all; as far as the public interest is concerned, they say with a well known man in New York, The public interest can go to Jericho. Now, they are supposed to be here to protect the public interest, but they have not done so. But there is an opposition here vigilant of the public interest-
And capable men, competent for any position.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Yes, and competent for any position, and who will take care of the public interest in due time. We find the Prime Minister of this country standing up as the apostle of protection and arguing in favour of fostering new industries in Canada. But there are two ways of fostering an industry. Does he tell me that the methods that they have undertaken is a proper way of doing it ? If they were initiating this thing nearly a year ago, as we now know, why did they not announce it on the public platform last year ? Why did they not confess that they were protectionists, and intended to build up an iron industry in this country ? They were ashamed of it, they could not justify themselves before their own free trade supporters ; therefore, they covered it up, and it would have remained covered up until to-day, this contract would have been issued in this way that the minister now repudiates, were it not that there is in this House a vigilant opposition who looks after the public interest. But this is not the way to encourage an iron and steel industry. Let the government announce some general policy, just as they announced their policy in regard to bounties on iron production, and let there be competition between manufacturers. Let the government lay down a general policy which will encourage the steel rail industry in this country. But they did not want to do it in that way, they were ashamed to do it in that way. any they buried it, and kept it hid during the election, and it would have been kept hid during this present session had not this debate brought it to light. Now the government come here, one section defending themselves, taking refuge behind an order in council, the other defending themselves behind a contract supposed to have been executed, but which has not been executed.

They do not know where they are. One moment they are behind the order in council, another moment they are behind the contract. Then we are told the contract lias not been executed. If the contract had been signed as it was drawn up Mr. Clergue would have had the benefit of it. Under that contract every one of these rails could have been rolled in the United States or in England. That is the way this government, who call themselves protectionists, now go to work to encourage new industries in this country. They have a law department and they have a minister who does business in that way ; they are all so incompetent that when a contract is drawn there is no provision made in it for doing what they profess to desire. They drew up what they called a protectionist contract, but for some reason or other they did not wish to utilize it before the election took place, they did not wish to let the public know that they had become protectionists.

The last time this item was discussed, the Minister of Railways laid what we all supposed was the contract on the Table. He defended that contract from one end of it to the other as a contract in the interests of the country. He said the price was good and favourable, that it was the lowest price at which the rails could be purchased. He stated that the general opinion was that rails were not on a falling market, but on a rising market. Now, as it happens, at that time there had been a large sale of English rails, English manufacturers had not been able to overtake the demand, and consequently they were not selling further rails. In the States production had overtaken the demand, consequently the price of rails was steadily falling. In the States rails had fallen within two months from $35 to $20 a ton, at the date on which the minister made this contract, he paid $7 a ton, more than the price for Which he could have got rails. Now, as Liberal-Conservatives and as protectionists, there is no reasonable limit to which we on this side of the House would not go to establish and protect a steel industry in this country. The difference between the two parties is that the Liberal-Conservatives would have made this contract openly, and adopted it as part of their policy. The government made this contract secretly, they covered up their contract and did not want the country to know it. There is the clearly defined difference between the two parties. Now let me show you that our contention was right as to the prices, and that the minister made his contract in a falling market. The price of manufactured pig iron in Canada during July, and up to the 28th of August, delivered at the Hamilton furnace, was $23 a ton; from the 28th of August to the 20th of September, it was $20 a ton ; from the 20th September onwards to October, and to the end

of the year, it was $18 a ton ; and to-day it is about $17 a ton. So there is a difference as between $23 and $17 a ton for the raw material. The price of rails in England kept up for some time, but no English rails were sold on this continent because American rails were bought, the price being so much lower. The hon. minister makes a contract amounting to about $4,000,000, he lays it on the Table- an assumed contract-we discuss it for one whole afternoon rather warmly on both sides of the House, and he comes here now and says that he never read the contract and that probably he might have signed it without reading it if this discussion had not come up. If $4,000,000 contracts are signed as a matter of course by the hon. minister without being read or discussed, because I take it for granted that none of the hon. minister's colleagues saw this contract or knew that it was a five years' contract, but himself, I think we can form a pretty fair opinion of how the enormous expenditure of this country is being carried on. I do not think it is possible to find, in any business, a transaction of this kind. If the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals buys hundreds of thousands of tons of rails at an advance of $7 a ton on the regular price, and defends his price as a reasonable one, then, I say he is not competent for the position he tills and the country may very well be shocked and startled as to what they may expect from the finances of the Intercolonial Railway, when a full knowledge of what has been done is exposed. The prices now are lower and there was every prospect of their continuing low at the time the contract was made. The loss on that contract to-day as between the price at which it was made and the price at which steel rails can be purchased-to-day they are up $2 a ton the Prime Minister says-is $200,000. A few days ago rails were selling at $25 a ton, delivered at Montreal, rails of the same character and quality as the rails agreed to be supplied to the government. Now, if these rails are not delivered this year, is the balance of the contract still to continue in force ? Is there a contract still for 25,000 tons of steel rails a year with the Sault Ste. Marie mills, or may other steel plants that are being built in other parts of the country, notably in Nova Scotia, compete for the balance of the 100.000 tons of rails wanted on the Intercolonial Railway during the next four years, or, has Mr. Clergue obtained that contract and can he till it by subletting the contract to the Nova Scotia steel works to manufacture the rails for him there ? There is nothing in the contract that would prohibit that. Personally I hope Mr. Clergue will be able to fill the contract. I do not think anything more important in the interests of Canada could happen than the establishment of prosperous steel works in this country. I would vote for giving, ns a bonus, the difference of $7 a ton for four or five years if by doing so, we could establish steel industries in Sault Ste. Marie and other parts of the country. W'liat 1 do object to, is having a secret contract made within three or four weeks of the election, on the face of it a suspicious fact, concealed from this House and in regard to which, with the greatest difficulty information has been drawn out. The members of the government, other than the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, were not aware of what that contract was, and I do not wonder that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has placed himself in a position which is so humiliating to himself, to the members of the government and to the members of this House, as he lias done to-day in the lame way in which he has tried to explain away this matter.

I do not understand what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Osier) means by his reference to a secret contract. It is not the habit of the various departments of the government, when a contract is made, to blazon it through the press, or to publish it in the newspapers. Contracts are being made day after day and month after month, and when parliament meets and information is desired with respect to any of these contracts, that information is, as a matter of course, brought down, but, when the hon. gentleman speaks as he did of a secret contract, as implying something wrong in this transaction, I want to tell him that this contract has been made in precisely the same manner as a thousand other contracts are made and that the word ' secret ' does not convey any such reproach as the hon. gentleman seems to imply in his remarks.
The amount of the contract has very much to do with it. There may be thousands of contracts, but here is a contract for $4,000,000 not communicated to this House.
And for five years.

Tlie magnitude of the contract does not touch the question of secrecy. Most of the contracts that are made are secret contracts. It is not usual to publish contracts in the newspapers unless there may be some special reason for it, and there is no such reason in the present transaction. I am reminded that one of my colleagues in the ministry announced in a public speech that it was proposed to aid the establishment of a steel manufacturing enterprise at Sault Ste. Marie, and therefore there was no secrecy such as the hon. gentleman seeks to imply. I have great difficulty in discovering what it is that hon. gentlemen opposite object to in this transaction, almost as much difficulty as some of them seem to have in understanding the nature of the transaction. My hon. friend the leader of

the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), referred to a difference which he and I had in respect to the position of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company in relation to the manufacture of rails. There is really no substantial difference between the hon. gentleman and myself. What he suggested in a jjrevious debate, because he did not go so far as to make an emphatic statement, was, that at the time this transaction occurred the Dominion Iron and Steel Company were prepared to make steel rails. If that was not the object of the hon. gentleman's observation then he had no purpose at all in making it. I do him the justice to say that he did not make the emphatic statement but rather the suggestion.

I think my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Fielding) has misunderstood what I said. I said that in the later months of 1900, the Dominion Iron and Steel Company made known to the public that they proposed to manufacture steel rails.

I am coming to that. I do the hon. gentleman the justice to say that it was a passing thought and that he did not emphasize it, but, unless his purpose was to suggest that at the time we made this contract the Dominion Iron and Steel Company were in a position to be competitors of Mr. Clergue, the observation of the hon. gentleman did not seem to have any bearing on the debate. He alluded to au issue of stock that was made for the purpose of enabling the company to engage in the manufacture of rails, and I reminded him, speaking entirely from memory, that that issue of stock had only been made within a couple of weeks of the time at which he spoke, and that therefore the Dominion Iron and Steel Company could not have been in a position then, or months before, to engage in that enterprise. He said that in December a prospectus, or a document of some kind, was issued announcing that the Dominion Iron and Steel Company were going to engage in the manufacture of rails. I am prepared to accept that as correct. But, what are the facts of this transaction ? In June, Mr. Clergue approached the government with a proposition, in the month of August the matter was discussed in council informally and agreed to, it was reported on formally by the Minister of Railways and Canals in September, the order in council was signed in October, and according to my hon. friend's statement, it was not until December that the Dominion Iron and Steel Company ever whispered that they had any intention of making rails. Therefore, there is no question whatever of competition between these two companies. Now, I have a difference of opinion with my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Borden)-if it be not too serious a statement for me to make as applied to a member of the legal profession-I have a difference of opinion with my hon. friend (Mr. Borden) regarding Mr. FIELDING.
his interpretation of the law of contracts, and I am a layman and he is an eminent lawyer. Now," what is the position ? We have had introduced into this debate unfortunately a document which should never have been brought down to this House. I say that the bringing down of that document was a piece of carelessness. It was not a contract, it was not signed. As it turned but it did not even represent the terms upon which the minister was prepared to make the contract.
Why did he tell us there was a contract made ?

The hon. Minister of Railways stated at the beginning that there was an understanding for a period of five years but that there was no explicit contract, and in the end that statement proved to be correct.

In his speech on the 9th of April he said :
We made a contract with this company.
Is that not plain enough English ?
The MINISTER OB' FINANCE. The Minister of Railways at that time no doubt was under the impression that a contract had been made. He tells you frankly now that he found that was a mistake. He had clearly in his mind the nature of the whole agreement from beginning to end. He spoke in the light of that, and his first statement was entirely a correct description of the arrangement he made with Mr. Clergue. I do not blame hon. gentlemen opposite for calling attention to the production of that document, because it was a thing that was irregular and which should not have occurred, but if we want to understand the merits of the question we will dismiss that entire ly from our minds. It is not a contract. It is a draft contract which was never executed. It is of no more value in; this discussion than any piece of waste paper. The only outstanding document which binds the government in this matter is the order in council. There is nothing else and why discuss anything else that does not exist ? The one obligation is the order in council, and what does that provide ? My hon. friend the leader of the opposition treats it as amounting to the same thing as a five years' contract. I may tell him that the difference between that order in council and a five years' contract is as the difference between a thing that is legal, and a thing that iis not legal. I can tell the hon., gentleman (Mr. Borden) that if we had made a five years' contract in the terms wbich; he implies in such a contract as that draft contract purported to be, I can tell him that would have been illegal. I tell him that it could not have been enforced by Mr. Clergue, and I can tell him that it could not have been enforced by the government of the country unless it were supplemented by a

parliamentary appropriation. I can tell the hon. gentleman tliat it was no contract at all.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Oil.

My hon. friend (Mr. Borden) differs from me there. I do not like to quote law books, but I will have to do so to help my hon. friend. There is the famous case of Churchward and the Queen which determines this question and against the opinion of the leader of the opposition I will quote such an eminent authority as Chief Justice Cockburn. This was a case in which it was claimed that a contract made with the Lords of the Admiralty for a mail service continuing from year to year, to be terminated on notice, should be a binding contract. That was disputed by the authorities and the determination of the courts in England was that it was not a legal and binding contract and that it could not be enforced by either side. I hate to have to read a law book ; it is not in my line, but since I made the statement one of my colleagues handed; me the book and said I was clearly right, and here is the law to support it: I stated the fact and now I have the law to back up my statement. I read from the judgment in Churchward against the Queen, which says :
Therefore, when we come to consider whether there is to be implied from the other terms of this contract and intention on the part of the Lords and the Admiralty to bind the Crown in the event of parliament not providing the funds, let us see what the position of all parties concerned would he, if, after parliament had refused to find the funds to satisfy the exigency of this contract, the Lords of the Admiralty had taken upon themslves, nevertheless, to continue to employ the contractor. In the first place, the government would have to put itself in a state of antagonism to parliament, inasmuch as it would have set the authority of parliament at defiance. In the second place, the head of a public department would continue to employ a public contractor, without the means of paying him ; for when it is said that possibly in the future parliament may find funds, one can hardly suppose that a public minister would be warranted in assuming such a possibility, when, so far as experience had shown, parliament has refused to find the funds; and I must say, it appears to me that to employ a public contractor without the means of payment, even if he were willing to be so employed, would be a course of proceeding altogether derogatory to the dignity of the Crown and to the honour of the country. In the third place, the contract certainly could not be enforced under such circumstances, I mean enforced by the public department. Suppose that parliament refused for the coming year to find the funds wherewith to remunerate Mr. Churchward, he, under such circumstances, would be entitled to say , ' as I cannot look to you, the other contracting parties, as i am not sntitled to look to the Crown, as I can only look to parliament, and parliament refuses to find the funds to pay me, I am not bound to go on.* I take it, if the other contracting parties then endeavoured to enforce the contract, equity would relieve the contractor from the obligation
to obey it; and if an action were brought at law, I doubt very much, indeed, whether a court of law would not say that the providing of the funds by parliament was a condition precedent to the fulfilment, or necessity of fulfilling, the contract.
In this case, if the minister will allow me, as there bad been no money voted there was no contract at all for the first year, or for any other.
And there was no money voted when we made this contract.
But you took great credit for that contract a moment ago.

If hon. gentlemen opposite are right we are making a contract to bind /us for five years, but we have no funds for five years and therefore in the words of the judgment I have read, there being no funds there could he no contract.
Then there is no contract.

I am very sorry that it falls to an untutored layman to have to explain the law to my friends opposite, but I happen to have bad' occasions in times past to know that such was the law. I know very well that if we make a contract for five years it is not a legal and binding contract, and we had that fact iu mind when we were so framing the order in council that we should make a contract-
Oh.

Yes ; that we should make a contract for one year, because we have the legal right to make it to the extent of one year, but as respects future years we determined that we should simply empower the minister to make the contract year after year ; not one contract, but five separate and distinct contracts made from year to year.

If there was no object in having a four year's contract, what was the use of getting in any references to it If there was no necessity or intention of binding one side or the other on a five years' contract, why should you encumber this contract with the four year's clause ?

As I stated before, it is the difference between recognizing the authority of parliament, and failing to recognize the authority of parliament. I do not hesitate to say that if there should be a change of government to-morrow and if the new ministry should make up its mind that that was not a judicious contract to make, they would not be bound to continue that contract, but I say we are morally bound, believing it to be a good arrangement. If Mr. Clergue supplies these rails manufactured in Canada-because the

suggestion that they are to be supplied from any other source is preposterous-if Mr. Clergue should supply these rails manufactured in Canada, up to the standard required and in all respects carries out his side of the arrangement, X would consider that we are morally bound to continue giving him these contracts for a jjeriod of five years. Therefore, I do not discriminate so carefully as probably my legal friends would between a legal contract and a moral contract; but the difference we made was just enough difference to keep within the law ; to make a one-year contract and to give Mr. Clergue the assurance of our goodwill for the encouragement of this enterprise, that he should continue to receive these orders for a period of five years. Now, 1 would like to ask hon. gentlemen in what other way they would have proceeded 1 If it is a legitimate arrangement in aiding an enterprise of that character-I am not discussing now whether it is protectionist or not because it is the thing itself we are concerned with, and not the name-if it is a legitimate thing to encourage the creation of a great manufacturing enterprise in Canada, while agreeing to take a giveu quantity of the product of the factory, how better could we proceed about it than by saying to Mr. Clergue, we will give you a contract for one year, and we will give you the assurance of our good-will for the continuing of this contract, if all goes well, for a further period of four years, making five years in all ?

I did not hear the beginning of this controversy, but what I did hear when I first came in was certainly most astonishing to me. The last time this contract was under discussion before the House, the statement was made that it was signed by the Minister of Railways and by tbe secretary of his department. I drew the attention of the Minister of Railways, and particularly the Finance Minister, to the fact that the contract was one for five years, and I enlarged upon that fact. I enlarged upon the fact that the government had entered into a contract, contrary to the pledges again and again made by them when they were in opposition, that a contract of the magnitude of this one should have a sum of money voted for it and should receive the consent of parliament before being entered into by the government. I drew their attention to that fact again and again, in the course of my remarks before all the members of the government, who are here at this moment ; and to my astonishment 1 find, according to the statement of these hon. gentlemen to-day, that no contract has been entered into except for one year only, but that if Mr. Clergue performs tbe conditions and furnishes the rails for this year, there is a moral obligation, but no contract binding upon them, to take the rails from him from year to year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

speechtext: Exactly; that is it-if we get an appropriation from parliament for it.

When was it that the hon. gentleman arrived at that conclusion ? How is it that it did not strike them the last time this matter was discussed V But, when they find that the people of this country are likely to weigh them for making such a bargain and going back on the promises they made again and again in this House, that no such contract should he made unless the money for it was voted, and unless they receive a mandate of this House to make it, they state that no contract has been signed, but that the order in council was passed-that the authority was given to the minister to make the contract. It may be that he has signed it, and that the officers of the department have signed it, but that it has not been fully executed. What more authority is it possible to get from the government of this country to enter into a contract than an order in council on a memorandum from the head of the department ? That would be binding on the government if the contract was never signed by the Minister of Railways, for he had the authority to sign it. We are told that there is no such thing as a contract by the government for two or three years- that a contract is only binding if the money is voted by this House. This is a new doctrine. Again and again, hundreds and thousands of times, the people of this country have been bound by contracts for two, three, five or ten years. It is true that these hon. gentlemen, when they came into power, under a technicality cancelled a large number of contracts to which the Governor General's signature was attached, and which they were legally as well as morally bound to carry out. But now, after giving the Minister of Railways the full sanction of the Governor in Council to enter into a contract, and although the minister may have affixed his signature to the contract, and the secretary of the department may have done the same, they say : There is no obligation upon him, except a moral one, to carry out the contract, because tbe money has not been voted, but if Mr. Clergue performs the first part of his contract faithfully, we shall feel ourselves morally bound to carry out the rest of it. They are morally bound, at any rate, to take the 125,000 tons of rails. In other words, contrary to the professions they have made a hundred times throughout the country, they have entered into a bargain by which the people of this country are morally bound to the extent of $4,000.000, without competition, and morally bound to pay an excess over the market price of rails at the moment they bought them, of six or seven dollars a ton-flinging away about $150,000 of the money of this country on the 25.000 tons of rails which they are bound to take. It is true, they might have

telegraphed to the old country and ascertained the price at which steel rails could be got in England ; but at that moment, within a couple of weeks of an election, they entered into a contract for rails, at $32.60 a ton, when they could have bought them for cash at six or seven dollars a ton les^.
Where were they to be bought at that price ?
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In the New York market, and at the same time the market was notoriously at the highest point at which it was likely to be. They purchased the 25,000 tons for future delivery. What was the necessity of that ? If Mr. Clergue does not deliver the rails in August, are you bound to take them ? The whole transaction savours of being the most disgraceful contract that ever was entered into by any government in any country in the world.

The hon. First Minister said that the only question before the House was whether or not the government had done right or wrong in making a contract with a Canadian company for the manufacture of steel rails. I do not hold that that is the only question before the House-not by any means. If that were the only question before the House, and they had made a proper contract, there would be no complaint from this side provided the rails were needed. The hon. minister says that we had authority to make such a contract, because parliament voted the money. Well, parliament had not voted the money. It was upon the request of parliament to vote the . money that the discussion arose. It was not because parliament has voted the money, but because it had not, that we were asked to vote $500,000 for the purchase of steel rails and other plant. What I complain of is this, and I was somewhat amused at the warmth of the hon. Minister of Railways when referring to criticism from this side, especially those by the hon. member for East Grey and others. In the first place, the House was misled, or at any rate, not dealt with frankly. The impression was left on the House that a contract had been made for 25,000 tons steel rails only.

Surely my hon. friend will be fair enough to say that I explained that we have made an explicit contract for one year for 25,000 tons, and had an understanding with Mr. Clergue for the four succeeding years.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That was made subsequently.
No, that was when I made my first statement in this House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I will read the hou. gentleman's own words :
We made a contract with this company to deliver 25,000 tons of the quality and standard which we have been placing upon the road, a rail eighty pounds in weight, and we were to pay them $32.60 per ton, the delivery to commence in the first week in August and to continue at such a rate that we would be able to lay the rails before the snow fell.

Where were they to be delivered?
The MINISTER OF RAILWAY'S AND CANALS. They were to be delivered to us in Montreal- that is, in the preseut year. We have no permanent and explicit contract with them for the future, although in their proposal they asked us to give them a contract for a term of live years and to give thorn an order for 50,000 tons with which to commence their industry. We finally concluded to give them an order for 25,000 tons, and while we have no explicit contract with them for any term beyond the year in which we are now' entering, we have an understanding with them under which if they furnish us, as they engage to do, the rails of ihe quality and standard we require, and at the current prices in the English market, we are prepared to continue to take our rails from them.
Some bon. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.
Not that we are prepared to take any quantity of rails at any given price, but we are merely prepared to do our dealings with them.

I have always found my hon. friend pretty fair, and I would ask him whether, iu the view which I then had of the contract, and which I was entitled to have-not having read or seen the draft, or had it presented to me for execution, but having iu my mind the order in council passed on my recommendation-I could have made a franker or fuller statement?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I can only say that the question is whether the House was led to believe there was only a contract made for
25,000	tons for one year, when it now turns out that the understanding with the company was that the contract was to be continued for five years or in other words was to be for 125,000 tons in all.
I said that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. minister said that he had an understanding that the government would take the rails from them at the market value, but if not would go elsewhere. He now tries to get out of the difficulty by saying that the contract is not in harmony with the order in council, and that the order in council does not fairly leave the impression that there was a contract for five years. What does the merno-randum submitted to council say :
In order to justify the great cost which such works would entail, the company desired to obtain the assurance, to some extent, of a market before proceeding to incur furrher expen-

diture, and they submitted a proposal that the government should give them a contract for the supply to the government railways of 50,000 tons of steel rails in the year 1901, and 25,000 tons annually for four years after.
Further on it is stated :
The minister further states that owing to the pressure of other matters and his own absence from Canada, he has been unable to bring this proposition formally before Your Excellency in Council until now. It was, however, discussed informally before the cabinet towards the close of August, 1900, being favourably considered, and it was understood that a recommendation would be made and be submitted by the Minister of Railways and Canals on the basis of a contract for 25,000 tons to be supplied in 1901 at $32.60 a ton (the price then being paid by the Department of Railways and Canals under its rail contract for the current year), and for a similar quantity for the five years following.
Does not that memorandum submitted to council leave the impression that there was a contract for 325,000 tons for five years, of -which 25,000 tons were to be supplied in 1901, and a similar quantity each following year during four years. This is evidently what was submitted to council.
That is only the recital. Read the recommendation.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It recommends :
The minister recommends that authority he given for entering 'nto an agreement with the company for the supply to the government railways of 25,000 tons (2,240 pounds to the ton) of first quality of steel rails ol eighty pounds to the yard, and of section prescribed by the Department of Railways and Canals, such supply to commence in the month of June, 1901, and to be completed in the month of September following; delivery to be male either at Levis or Montreal (c.i.f.), as the department may direct, and so far as practicable, in equal quantities monthly, the price to he paid for the said rails so delivered to be fixed, as agreed upon, at $32.60 per ton, which, as above stated, is the price now being paid by the Department of Railways and Canals.

That is only for one year.
Mr. oPROULE (reading) :
The minister further recommends that he be authorized to contract yearly thereafter for the supply of a similar quantity of such rails during each succeeding year, for a term of five years, to be delivered either at. Halifax, Port Mulgrave, Ldvds or St. John, as may he required by the Department of Railways and Canals, the price for the said rails to he the price for the same quality of rails in the open market.
I leave that point, and wish to direct attention to another thing the hon. minister said. Another reason why we objected was, that the transaction was a large one to be undertaken without the consent of parliament. It is a transaction involving an expenditure of $4,000.000, and parliament was not consulted. And we have no information that the rails were urgently needed. We Mr. SPROULE.
contended that the Minister of Railways and Canals was not justified in making a contract involving $4,000,000 without consulting parliament beforehand, especially in view of the fact that he did not need the rails. And my contention was that these rails were purchased in the face of a falling market. The minister denies that. But I quote the summary giving four times a month, the market value of steel rails in New York. And he asks : Are we going to be guided by the New York market-we never looked at the New York market, but the English market. But, I would remind the hon. minister that in this explanation as to where he got his rails last year, he said :
Last year the rails were purchased by tender. They were furnished by two firms, a part by each, the Illinois Company and the Cambria Company.
Were not these American companies ? Did the hon. gentleman look to England then ? He defends himself in that case on the [DOT] ground that lie got them from the lowest tenderer. Is he disposed now to overlook the fact that the rails were at least $6.50 lower in the American market than in the English market ? And now he accepts a price $6.50 higher than the American market, and justifies it by saying that it was the standard of the English market. Can he defend that before the country ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) condemn it ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I do condemn paying $6.50 more for rails than they can be bought for in the open market.
Then the hon. gentleman does not want to see a Canadian industry established ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am as anxious as is the hon. gentleman to see the Canadian industry established ; but, I am not prepared to defend the minister entering into a contract by which he loses $200,000 of the money of the people of Canada in buying rails when he did not require those rails, and could have got them cheaper in the American than in the English market-for he only sets off one against the other. I condemn this contract further, because it was made when an election was going on-right in the midst of it. I say that that is improper. How do we know what subscription the hon. gentleman got in the face of that contract ? It is very suspicious, to say the least of it, for we know that these things are sometimes done. Here is a contract entered into privately, entered into at that particular time, entered into for a purpose concerning which we are not yet informed. We have a right to condemn it for all these reasons, it is our duty to condemn it, and I believe the country will condemn it as well.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.

After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.

I must say that I am at a great loss to understand just where we are at in reference to this contract. On the 9th of April, when discussing an item in the estimates for steel rails and fastenings, $500,000, the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. -Haggard) brought out from the Minister of Railways and Canals that there was a contract with the company of which Mr. Clergue seems to be the head
Brought out ? I stated the fact before the hon. member for Lanark had opened his mouth.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Then on the 9th of April the Minister of Railways and Canals stated that there was a contract with the company of which Mr. Clergue, as I understand, is the head, for the purchase of rails. The hon. -member for South Lanark asked to have the contract, tenders, &c., laid on the Table. On the 10th of April we find, when this item comes up for discussion, that there is laid upon the Table what purports to be a contract made between the government and this company. In the discussion on that contract, by the hon. member for South Lanark, after referring in general terms to the contract, and (the price to be paid for these rails :
The Minister of Railways and Canals states then that it is just what I stated it was.
In the discussion which took place in connection with that contract the Minister of Railways and Canals, when the question of date comes up, says :
Look at the agreement, I think you will see the date mentioned.

Oh, yes; the 9th of October, 1900.
We .'find further on in the discussion that the Minister of Railways and Canals states that he is quite satisfied to have the document examined, and investigated, and turned over in every shape and form. Later on he says :
Well, now, what are the terms of that contract? If it is open to criticism, then let the hon. gentleman criticise it, as it is his right to do. Do the terms state that we are to pay to- this Lake Superior Power Company any price it may ask?
Showing that the Minister of Railways and Canals, on the 10th of April, was familiar with the contract which was then being discussed by the member for South Lanark. Then, in reply to the member for Bothwell (Mr. CHancy), the Minister of Railways and Canals refers again to the contract, and says :
Does it prove that when the contract was made, the price was higher than the market price which existed at that time?
Again, when the question is brought up as to the contract extending over a period of five years, he says :
When we come to settle up for the next year's supply of rails, if the contract which has been entered into is carried out and the rails are delivered, we have to ascertain what the market price is in England, and the market price in England is a safe guide.
I have quoted to a small extent from the speech of the Minister of Railways and Canals made on the 10th of April, to show that at that time he certainly was familiar with the terms of the contract which was laid on the Table of this House, and he was able to discuss -it with the hon. gentlemen who were speaking about this contract. We find that on the 11th of April, although the contract was spread broadcast throughout the country as being the contract that had been entered into between this government and the Lake Superior Power Company, we never found until to-day that that contract was repudiated by the Minister of Railways and Canals or by any member of the government. Now what spectacle do we find to-day ? We find that the contract is repudiated, we find the Minister of Railways and Canals saying that there is no contract existing as between the Lake Superior Power Company and the government of Canada. We find the Minister of Finance jumping to the rescue of the Minister of Railways, we find him getting into the saddle and giving a horseback opinion on a very important question of law ; we find him quoting from this case of Churchward vs. the Queen, cited in one Queen's Bench Reports, page 173. Iam not going to deal with that case, I have no doubt some other hod. gentlemen on this side will show the Minister of Finance that it would be well for him not to give horseback opinions on questions of law, nor to quote cases which are not at all applicable to the matter under discussion.
Now the Prime Minister has said that the question -is whether this government are wise to enter into a contract for the manufacture of steel rails. I humbly submit that that is not the question. The question now is, where is this contract ? Is there a contract, or is there not a contract ? We find the ministers disagreeing on that point. One says there is a contract, another says there is not a contract, that we have no contract before the House. Now I would like to ask what constitutes that contract ? Is it simply the correspondence which took place between the Lake Superior Power Company and the Minister of Railways, and the order in council that was passed in connection with -these rails ? I say if that is a contract, then the government have not been entirely fair to this House when, on the 10th of April, they laid this agreement before the House which they now say was never signed by the Lake Superior Power Company, and led -this House to believe that that was the contract in force between that company



and the government. These steel rail contracts do not seem to be handled very well by the hon. gentlemen. We had an experience in former years of steel rail contracts entered Into by these hon. gentlemen. Now 1 say that the hon. member for South Lanark was quite justified in bringing this matter to the attention of the House and of the public. He found, in going into that estimate, that suddenly, after the election writs were issued, a contract involving some $4,000,000 was entered into by this government. I was surprised that the Minister of Finance should state in this House that any minister would bring down a contract of that Importance, involving that large amount of money, without giving the contract any consideration, and try to justify his course by saying that it was brought down through carelessness. I say if that sort of carelessness is going to exist in contracts involving $4,000,000, it is time that the public were made fully aware of It.

I hardly think the hon. gentleman is doing me justice. I did not say there was any carelessness with regard to the making of a contract, I said a document which was not a contract and which had no bearing on the matter, had been brought down; but I did not say that there was any carelessness in the making of any contract.

I understood the hon. Minister of Finance to say that this document, which was laid on the Table, which was given to this House as a contract between the Lake Superior Power Company and the government of Canada, and which w*is discussed all one afternoon by this House, as if it were a contract that was in existence, was brought down through carelessness.
I say so now, because it was not a contract.
Then why was it brought down as purporting to be a contract ?
Through the carelessness of an official.
Whose carelessness ?

It was brought down through the carelessness of some official. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has stated that he had never signed a contract. If it had been an executed contract and the minister did not know it, that would have been carelessness, but a document was brought down which the minister had not signed. There is no proof of carelessness on the part of a minister there.
Then it was a piece of gross carelessness on some one's part. Now, we find that this contract for 125,000 tons of rails, to be supplied to the Dominion of Canada during a period of five years, was

laid on the Table, as the hon. Minister of Finance says, through the carelessness of somebody. I say that this is a most important contract, and while I do not wish to discuss now the merits of the contract, because I feel that we have not got the contract on the Table, so that we can properly and intelligently discuss the details of it, yet I say that we find that this company received from the Dominion of Canada $6 per ton bounty and $1 per ton bounty from the Ontario government, making a bounty of $7 per ton, or a total bounty of $S75,000 on the 125,000 tons of rails to be delivered to this government, and we find that, apart from that, they are given a price upon which there is certainly a difference of $5 or $6 per ton between the market price to-day and the price as set out in this contract. I wish to say that I think the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals .should not be so careless in the future. He should not deal with contracts involving such a large amount of money in a careless way in which it has been shown to-day he has dealt with this contract. Now, in reference to the order in council, I have not the order before me, but, if we are to take it for granted that the contract is contained in that order in council and in the correspondence which the Lake Superior Power Company sent to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, then, it does seem to me that the order in council does not provide for the manufacture of these rails in the Dominion of Canada. Certainly, the contract does not provide for that. I think that even the hon. Minister of Finance, as a layman assuming to deal with legal questions, would come to the conclusion, if he reads the contract which was laid on the Table, that the operative part of the contract does not compel the manufacture of these rails in the Dominion of Canada. Hon. gentlemen may say that the recital in the contract says something about the manufacture of these rails in Canada, but I would just say that where the operative part of a contract uses language which admits of no doubt, it cannot be contracted by the recital, and I say that the operative part of this contract is clear, and that there is nothing in it which compels the manufacture of these rails in Canada. I think it is due to this committee that we get a definite statement from the hon. Minister of Railways as to the terms of this contract and that the order in council and correspondence, or whatever they say constitutes this contract, be laid on the Table.

There are a few points in this in regard to which it strikes me it is worth while detaining the committee a few minutes to say something on. First of all, in the eloquent words of an American congressman, I would like to see ' where we are at.' Shortly, on the 9th of April, we were told by the responsible minister that there was a contract. Then, be-

fore the discussion was through, it was discovered from him that this was in writing ; then, according to the rule, he was asked to produce it. On the 10th he produced what was said to be a contract. It seems, to-day, from the revelation that has been made, that it is more than doubtful that any executed contract has so far been shown to be in existence. Well then, these are two positions. In the third place, today, the hon. minister takes the position that he stopped the execution of this contract by Mr. Olergue after the discussion on the 10th. I am mentioning these points to show the inconsistent position of the minister in regard to this matter. What happens to-day ? The right toon. Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) says there is no contract; he produces the order in council and toe bases an argument upon it to show that it only authorized a contract from year to year. Then, we have the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding), who says that it is clear there is no contract beyond the year, tout, he thinks there is a moral obligation, and yet, what do all these ministers of the Crown, the right hon. leader of the government among them, base the justification of this contract upon ? They based it upon the establishment of a steel rail manufactory in Canada. How ? By a contract encouraging it. If that is true, I would like to hear any successful manufacturer, or any reasonable man, contend for one moment that encouragement for one year would induce him to engage in the manufacture of rails. What do they want ? They want the assurance of a certain number of years. They must all agree to that. What is the logical consequence ? Either that the government have no notion of what they are about, or that they have been deceiving and misleading the gentleman who has undertaken to establish these works at the cost of a very large sum of money. That is clear. These are the two horns of the dilemma. I would like to know what position the government take upon that. I say that the intention from the contract, from the order in council, from the actions of the responsible minister, was, that they should make a bargain for 25,000 tons of rails this year with the Clergue syndicate, or the Lake iSuperor Power Company, whatever you may call them-I will call them the Clergue syndicate, because we know them by this name in the country-and they gave them to understand that they had a binding promise from the government of Canada that they were to have a contract for five years. The details of this were to be settled, how ? To be settled on the basis of the market price of rails each year in England. Are the government prepared to say that I am incorrect ?

I am prepared to say that they gave Mr. Clergue, 113i
the order in council for exactly what it contains, and that he was satisfied with it.
Is the hon. Minister of Finance prepared to say they gave him a copy of it ?
Yes, certainly, as already stated.
On the 12th of October, at Mr. Clergue's request, that was handed to him.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am very glad to get that answer. Why do you want to put it in the form of a contract at all, if the order in council is a contract ? Do you think for a moment that Mr. Clergue and the combination of capitalists who are putting millions into this enterprise would entertain the proposition at all if they did not believe in the good faith of the order in council ? Men who do not understand legal technicalities would understand that an order in council passed by the government pledges more than the ordinary legal contract, for it pledges the good faith of this country of ours. I am not discussing the merits of the agreement pro or con, but I say that if men put their money into an undertaking on the faith of a pledge given by the government of this country, then, if another government took the place of the government that made that pledge, I, for one, would insist on having its terms carried out, because the fair name and the good credit of the Dominion is at stake, and if these are not honoured, then we do not deserve to succeed as a young and respected nation. Each of the three ministers who spoke to-day disagreed from the other as to the contract, but they all agreed that the justification for it was to encourage the industry of steel rail-making in Canada. That is a thing dear to the hearts of Conservatives ; a doctrine they have promulgated in power and out of power since the adoption of the national policy, and a policy on which they are prepared to support the present government, so far as reason will allow. I do not think there will be a more surprised man in the Dominion than Mr. Clergue when he hears that the custodian of the good name of Canada, who has control of our finances, stated that there is only a moral obligation in it. There is no moral obligation on the government in one sense, but they have a financial obligation, and they have the moral obligation to maintain the good name of Canada. Although it may be politically to our advantage, I am sorry that the Minister of Railways changed his base as regards this contract, because except in one respect the contract he laid on the Table is a fair exposition of the terms of the order in council. Of course, whoever drew it up forgot to insert a clause to compel them to manufacture the rails in Canada.

I do not think that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Tisdale) wants to make a misstatement. It is not right for him to say that there has been a change of base in regard to this. There has been no change of base at all. The government propose to carry out in its entirety and in all good faith the understanding contained in that order in council. We are prepared to enter into a contract with Mr. Clergue in accordance with the terms of the order in council, and Mr. Clergue will tell you that he is absolutely confident with regard to that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There certainly was a change of base, because the minister withdrew the contract he intended to have executed.
It was not the contract I intended.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Up to to-day we thought it was the contract. After carefully reading that supposed contract, and comparing it with the order in council, I say it is a fair exposition of the terms of the order in council, except that whoever prepared it forgot-I will not say neglected -to put in a clause compelling them to make the rails in Canada. The contract is a peculiar one. As regards the 25,000 tons of rails it is positive, but as regards the remainder, it is only provisional, and it could not be anything else. It certainly is a covenant to contract with the Clergue syndicate for other supplies of rails. Now, I wish to ask the Minister of Railways if he ever before this asked this House to vote him a large sum of money where a contract was to be made under an order in council, until he brought down the contract duly executed ? I know of no case in which that was not done. It was done with regard to the Drummond County Railway, and it is always done. I, for one, shall insist that any government, before it asks for an appropriation to carry out a contract for more than a single year, shall submit this contract to the House, and have it approved. That is only fair and proper.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I either did not make myself plain or the minister misunder-Mr. TISDALE.
stood me. I say where there is an order in council passed, upon which a contract is founded which extended beyond a single year, that contract is always brought down. For that we have the good constitutional reason that beyond the actual vote parliament is supreme, and until parliament gives its sanction it has no binding effect.
Hear, hear.

True, it has no binding effect, but on the other hand the good faith and credit of the country may be pledged under the order in council. We should have the contract. There is no better illustration of the necessity of that, than what has occurred here. The minister told us what the contract was and when his officer reduced it to writing it is only after two days' discussion that we find the minister was mistaken. The leader of the opposition made an extremely fair request of the Minister of Railways, when he said that before this vote passes we should at least have the agreement before us so that we can pronounce upon it. The time is getting short, I hope, before we shall prorogue, and if the executory contract is produced, I for one would be willing to treat it as an exceptional case, and vote to pass it without the signatures of the parties to it, though I think the constitutional rule should be to require the signatures to contracts before they are submitted to parliament. In conclusion, let me ask the ministry, what are they going to do about it ? They say there is no contract. The Prime Minister says there is one for a year. The Finance Minister says there is nothing after that but a moral obligation. If there is no contract after that, and if Mr. Clergue is not assured that good faith is going to be kept with him, he cannot go on. On the good faith of that agreement, as he believes it to be, he is asking capitalists to invest millions of dollars in these works which he is seeking to establish ; and if there is nothing after the first year but a moral obligation, the government are treating Mr. Clergue unfairly. That is not the way the business of Canada should be conducted. I am both surprised and grieved at the way in which the minister has managed this contract, because I did not think he allowed agreements to be completed in the way he has mentioned to-day ; and I agree with the hon. member who has last spoken, that if he does, he should change his practice. I know what the practice of the departments under the old government was, and it should be the same under this government and all governments. In the case of all important contracts, after the law officers have been consulted in regard to them, the responsible minister should see them and examine them before they are sent out to be executed by the other party. The Minister of Railways said to-day that he frequently did

not look at contracts until they came back executed, and then, if he found any change to be necessary, he sent them out again. I say that is a dangerous practice, and does not indicate good government management in the eyes of the people. As a business man, I would expect when a contract was signed, that it was settled ; and if you sent it back to me a second time, I would be suspicious. I have in my lifetime signed at least a dozen contracts coming from the different government departments, and I have never known such a case as this before. A contract is usually sent to be signed by the outside party first, so that there will be no question about the Crown being bound until the outside party is bound. All important contracts should go to the minister for his approval before they are sent out at all, and then there will be no mistake. Let me apply that principle to this case. Mr. Clergue has no doubt shown this agreement to his colleagues and to capitalists, as he had a right to do, and lie would say to them, ' There is my contract.' Are we to be told that a document involving the expenditure of $4,000,000 of public money, is to be sent out to be executed before being approved of by the minister, and, after being executed by the other party to it, is to be sent out again ? I do not wish the minister to misunderstand me. In small matters the same course is not necessary; but in important cases such as this, I think It is worth while to have the contract properly examined and properly certified, the minister becoming responsible for them before they are sent out to be signed at all.

With respect to the legal contention which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance put forward, I do not know that the House need concern itself very much as to that. I may say a word or two about it before I sit .down. But as the hon. Minister of Fijiance thinks that the case of Churchward vs. the Queen is on all fours with this case, I would like to point out the particular circumstances which induced parliament to refuse to grant the money in that case ; and I should imagine that the hon. gentleman would not be very much obliged to the gentleman who suggested to him that that case was in point here.
Would that affect the principle, does my hon. friend think ?

I will deal with the legal principle later on. I am dealing now with the parliamentary principle which was laid down in the House of Commons, namely, that parliament would not vote the money because there was corruption.
No no. I have the speech of Mr. Gladstone.

Well, I have a resolution of the committee with regard to
it, and I suppose that is as good as Mr. Gladstone's speech. My hon. friend the Solicitor General will have ample opportunity to give us Mr. Gladstone's speech, which the House will probably receive with a great deal of interest. It appeared in evidence before the committee
Will my hon. friend permit me to ask him whether he has reference to what took place in 1858, 1860, or 1883, because the matter came up three successive times ?

I am aware that it came up three successive times ; but it wais always tire same matter. There is a very full and detailed statement of the case in Mr. Todd's book on Parliamentary Government in England, at pages 772 to 780. In that case there was a contract subsisting in 1859. It was to expire in 1863. An agreement was made to extend it until 1870, and the question arose with respect to the renewal of that agreement from 1863 to 1870. I am now quoting from Mr. Todd's work, at page 772 :
It appeared In evidence before the committee (which investigated the renewal of the contract) that on the eve of the last general election, when the extension of his contract was under consideration at the Treasury,' Mr. Churchward volunteered his support, as an influential elector for Dover, ^to Captain Carnegie, one of the Lords of the Admiralty, if he should become a candidate for that borough. lie did this on the expectation that his contract was to be renewed. The committee, however, fully exonerated all the officers, both of the Admiralty and of the Treasury, with whom the decision in regard to this contract rested, from being influenced by any corrupt or political motive in granting the same. They did, indeed, consider that the conduct of Mr. Murray, the private secretary to the First Lord of the Admiralty, was open to grave censure; but they had not sufficient evidence to show that any member of the government was cognizant of the communications between Mr. Murray, Mr. Churchward and Captain Carnegie.
While declaring themselves most fnxious for the fulfilment of all engagements entered into 'n good faith between the government and private individuals, the committee, nevertheless, submitted to the House ' whether Mr. Churchward, in having resorted to corrupt expedients affecting injuriously the character of the representation of the people in parliament, has not rendered it impossible for the House of Commons, with due regard to its honour and dignity, to vote the sums of money necessary to fulfil the agreement to extend his contract from June 20, 1863, to April 26, 1870.'
A change of ministry having taken place since the last renewal of this contract, the incoming administration in deference to the foregoing report, and to the general opinion of the House, tacitly concurring therein, refused to recognize the amended contract, which entitled Mr. Churchward to a fixed sum per annum, hut permitted him to continue to conduct his postal service under the former contract, under which he was ordinarily allowed a smaller amount, but was authorized to make extra charges for certain special services. This contract would remain in force until June, 1863,

and was free from objection of any kind, it not having been included in the censure of the committee.
Then there is a reference to certain efforts made by friends of Mr. Churchward. They brought forward on the 27th March, 18(30, a motion in parliament resolving :
That the House having considered the report and evidence presented by the committee, is of the opinion that the contract entered into on April 26th, 1839, between the Lords of the Admiralty and J. D. Churchward ought to be fulfilled.
The Chancellor of the Exchequer, Mr. Gladstone, opposed this motion, declaring that the impartial finding of the committee was entitled to respect; that independently of their report it was clear from the evidence that corrupt expedients, affecting injuriously the dignity of parliament, had been resorted to to obtain a renewal of this contract. Under these circumstances, he added, the present ministry were under no obligation to carry out the new contract, and the House were not bound to vote the money, for the executive has no constitutional authority to make a contract binding on the House of Commons.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.
Whereupon the motion was negatived on division.
That is the question.

My hon. friend does not seem to understand the point I am making. In ordinary circumstances, the executive always feels bound, as a matter of good faith, to ask parliament to vote the moneys unless some circumstances have occurred.
That is the point.

The Minister of Finance did not take that position this afternoon. He said distinctly that it would, be perfectly proper, for an incoming administration to repudiate this contract if it thought It was not in the public interest. I say that there is no support for any such doctrine to be found except on some such ground as that stated in the case I have quoted. The legal liability is one thing-although the case which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance referred to does not support the proposition he made-the question of legal 1 liability is one thing and that of good faith another. It is always competent for a government, if it sees fit to do so, to repudiate liability, because the Crown cannot be sued without its own consent. A fiat upon a petition of right can be refused and so the liability can be avoided. As a matter of fact about forty petitions of right have been standing before the Postmaster General during the last two years, on which he has not granted a fiat, and the petitioners have obtained no satisfaction up to the present.
Could a fiat in such a case be enforced legally ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I will read the hon. gentleman something about that by-and-by.
Take this case then and answer my question.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
that kind must be implied as a part of every contract, but that is a mere dictum, and we have against it the decision of sir Alexander Cockburn that if there had been no question of that kind in the way, the petitioner would have been entitled to relief.
But the broad question we are discussing here is whether this or any government of this country, in the language of the Minister of Finance, can, without any reason whatever, turn to one side this agreement with Mr. Clergue and say it is not in the interests of this country that such an agreement should be carried out. What were the facts in the case of that kind in the English House of Commons. At page 780 of Todd's Parliamentary Government is found the very case referred to, which my hon. friend the Minister of Finance mentioned-the case In which parliament virtually declared and found that a contract entered into by a preceding administration was not in the best interests of the country-the committee of the House reported its opinion that the contract had been unwisely entered into, that it had been given without sufficient regard to the interests of Canada, that a line of ocean steamers would have readily undertaken the new service on more favourable terms, and that the arrangement was altogether an impolitic and improvident one. Well, what was done with that contract ? Not only did the succeeding administration consider itself bound by it, but even when the company made default and was unable to carry out its contract, within the exact lines of the stipulations, the government did not take advantage of that, but gave the company further time to put itself in a condition to carry out its obligations ? That is a policy exactly the opposite of that which was laid by a member of the government this afternoon. I would not have thought it desirable to say anything with regard to this matter if it had not been for that very important announcement made by the Minister of Finance to-day as to the duty of this and succeeding administrations with respect to contracts of this kind.
I do not desire to occupy time further except to refer to a principle, which is distinctly laid down in England, that contracts of this kind should either be submitted in the fa'st instance to parliament or else contain a stipulation' that they should not become binding until parliament shall have pronounced on them. That is a course which the Minister of Railways did not see fit to pursue in this case. I will read the doctrine with regard to that, as held in England and laid down in this book of undoubted authority, and would respectfully ask the Minister of Railways to give heed to it; and I may say in passing that if parliament can repudiate, as the Minister of Finance says it can, an agreement to take the rails for the next four years, it can equally
repudiate any agreement to take the rails this year, because there was no appropriation by parliament to buy these rails, as X understand it. Therefore, if parliament could repudiate its agreement for the next four years, it could with equal good faith repudiate its agreement for this year.
By refusing to vote the money-certainly.
The hon. Minister of Finance would consider that in so doing it was acting within Its right ?
If parliament refuses to make the appropriation the contract fails.
And my hon. friend would consider that a government which would not stake its existence upon carrying out a contract of that kind would be doing Its duty ?
But we are going to stake our existence upon it.
But this afternoon the hon. gentleman took a different position.
No.

Then I do not understand what position he takes. I suppose he distinguishes between the duty of this administration and the duty of a succeeding administration. 'There is no such distinction to be found in any of the books, nor is there any principle upon which such a distinction could be made. The duty of the country in such matters is laid down by the authorities in England, as stated in this book, as follows :
In the interval between the execution of a contract and the application to parliament for vote in supply on account thereof, heavy expenses and liabilities are necessarily incurred by the contractors, so as to render it a matter of peculiar hardship and difficulty for the House, in the absence of any charge of fraud, misrepresentation or corrupt proceedings, to interpose and refuse to vote the moneys required to carry out a contract which has been entered into by government within the limits of its own authority.
I think that is sound common sense and sound reason. Parliament may think that a contract of that kind is not politic in the interests of the country, that it is a contract into which the government should not have entered ; but, seeing that the contractor has incurred expense on account of his faith in the honour of his country, parliament will not decline to pass the vote. At the same time, parliament should not be placed in a position of that kind. It should be allowed, in the first instance, to consider the contract before it is made. The authority I have already quoted proceeds :
Parliamentary control is thereby practically excluded in regard to an important branch of public expenditure. While it seems repugnant

to the principles of our constitution that the executive government should be free to enter into contracts binding the country for prolonged periods, and by anticipation, to the payment of vast sums, without the possibility of any effective parliamentary check beyond the disapproval after the evil had been accomplished, and when perhaps the ministers by whom the contract was made were no longer in office, nevertheless the committee were fully sensible of the difficulties attending any change of system which might result in a parliamentary canvass on behalf of competing candidates for a public contract.
Therefore, they recommend, and the English practice now is, in all such cases, that a stipulation be inserted in the contract that it should not be binding upon the country until the assent of parliament is obtained. That is a sound principle. It gives parliament the power and the right to exercise its discretion, and that is what the Minister of Railways should have done in this case. I regret to have felt called upon to trespass upon the attention of the committee so long, but I thought the subject worthy of the remarks I have made.

I think it is quite clear that our hon. friends on the other side are somewhat disappointed with the turn that this debate has taken. On the last day when this question was debated, they were evidently under the impression that a contract had been made which left the government open to severe censure. Listening to the remarks of the hon. gentlemen who have debated the question, I am forced to the conclusion that instead of devoting their attacks to the real transaction upon which the government has entered, they have devoted their attacks altogether to proving that the government ought to enter into a transaction which it has not entered into, and ought to go on and do something which it has not bound itself to do.
