My hon. friend from South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) was in grave fear lest the good faith of the government and the honour of Canada might be prejudiced by the fact that the government would not go on and make a' contract for four or five years longer, whereas the whole attack hitherto has been that the government had already done that which the hon. member for South Norfolk is now afraid will not be done. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has with considerable ability-as is his wont-quoted certain authorities for the information of the committee, which authorities have gone to show that when the government has entered into a contract the government was bound by the contract. Now, he need not have cited any considerable number of authorities to prove that, because I think we will all admit It
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton).

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question ? Does he hold that with the Minister of Finance that a succeeding administra-
tion might refuse to carry it out on the ground that it was an impolitic contract-
Improvident.
An improvident contract 1

I think I shall be able to meet my hon. friend's point when I come to discuss the question of what the contract is, which hon. gentlemen on the other side sedulously avoid placing before the committee. The contention of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition is that the successors of the government would be bound by a contract which the government has made. Unquestionably that is the case. And he points out that where a contract was repealed or was not assented to by a succeeding government, it was on account of the committee finding that there was a savour of corruption in connection with the contract; and, except for that, the government would be bound. We will agree to that. We will agree that any contract the government enters into is binding upon the House, and the good faith of the country. But the hon. gentleman will recognize that the principle which he laid down just before he resumed his seat, that when a contract is to extend over a fiscal yeai% it should receive the as- * sent of parliament, is a sound principle. We are all perfectly familiar with the idea that when a contract is made involving an expenditure of money which has not been voted by parliament, and extending beyond the fiscal year, it is not a binding contract under the law unless it has received the assent of parliament. Well, now, my hon. friend cited a case or two in which he referred to the judgments of certain learned judges as indicating what was binding upon the government and what was not. And, if I understood the purpose and desire of the hon. gentleman in quoting these expressions of opinion on the part of the judges, that purpose was to show that under circumstances similar to those actions would lie against the government if flats had been granted. I do not know whether he intended to leave that impression upon the minds of the committee oj; not, but if not, there was no point in the quotation of the authority. I think the hon. gentleman would hardly stand up here and pledge his professional reputation upon the statement that an action would lie against this government under the circumstances of this transaction.
Perhaps, if our hon. friends opposite will not find fault with us, it might be well to consider what the contract is. I think it will be very clear that the hon. gentlemen have been well advised in the conduct of this debate in endeavouring to divert the attention of the committee from the actual terms of the contract to something else which does not exist in the contract. The report of the Minister of Railways and Canals

contains the substance of the order in council, the order in council being merely paraphrase of the report. The minister says :
The undersigned, recognizing the benefits which the creation of an industry of such an extent and importance in Canada would necessarily bring directly in the employment of labour, the expansion of mining operations, and the transportation of crude materials and finished products, and, indirectly, in the development of numerous other industries by which this would be served, considers that the project is one which should receive all encouragement at the hands of the government,

I read the foregoing part and recital because it shows clearly what the minister and the government bad in their minds, and the purpose for which this order in council was passed :
-and he recommends that authority be given for entry into an agreement with the company for the supply to the government railways of 25,000 tons (2,240 pounds to the ton) of first quality steel rails of eighty pounds to the yard, and of section prescribed by the Department of Railways and Canals, such supply to commence in the month of June, 1901, and to be completed in the month of September following; delivery to be made either at Ldvis or at Montreal (c.i.f.), as the department may direct, and, so far as practicable, in equal quantities monthly, the price to be paid for the said rails so delivered to be fixed, as agreed upon, at $32.60 per ton, which, as above stated, is the price now being paid by the Department of Railways and Canals.
The minister further recommends that he be authorized to contract yearly hereafter for the supply of a similar quantity of such rails during each succeeding year for a term of five years, to be delivered either at Halifax, Port Mul-grave. Ldvis or St.. John, as may be required by the Department of Railways and Canals, the price for the said rails to be the price for the same quality of rails in the open market in Great Britain at the time when the order therefor is given by the Department of Railways and Canals.
This order in council authorizes the minister to make that contract for 25,000 tons of steel rails at $32.60 per ton for this year, and it authorizes him afterwards to enter into a distinct and separate contract each year for 25,000 tons of steel rails-at what price ? At $32.60 per ton ? No, but at the price in the open market, at what the rails may be worth. That is the contract the hon. gentleman entered into, that is the contract which the order in council authorizes, and nothing else.
Now, what is the transaction ? My hon. friend from South Norfolk (Mr. Tisdale) is disturbed, not on account of the policy of the transaction, not on account of the substance of the transaction, but he is disturbed, forsooth, not for fear that the Minister of Railways will enter into the agreement, but for fear that he won't. That is the criticism which the hon. gentleman addresses to this committee on behalf of his friends. I do not think that is the impression which the hon. gentleman's friends will endeavour to create in the country in
reference to this contract. They are endeavouring to create in the minds of the public the impression that an improvident contract has been made, and the hon. gentleman, on the other hand, is endeavouring to prove that we ought to go on and make this contract which they say is improvident. Now, this is what the Minister of Railways has recommended, and what the government has authorized him to do, first, to make a contract for the first year for 25,000 tons of rails at $32.60 ; secondly, that thereafter, in each year, he may make a separate and distinct contract. He has authority under the order in council to make that contract for 25,000 tons at the market price. Now, do we want the rails V We want 25,000 tons a year for five years for the government railway. Then, if we want 25,000 tons a year for the next five years, where in the name of common sense is the improvidence in contracting to buy them at the market price ? There is no money lost in that transaction. What is the consequence of the transaction ? One consequence of the transaction is, that instead of reserving the right to buy German rails, or English rails, or American rails, the government has said in the contract that it will authorize the Minister of Railways to buy Canadian rails. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has said that in the negotiations in connection with this matter it was stated to these gentlemen : If you go on and establish your rolling mill, the Minister of Railways will take rails from you in order to establish this industry, paying you the market price. The people of Canada will not lose one single copper. There is no financial loss in buying the rails at what they are worth in the open market. The $200,000 of loss, which my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) refers to, is simply a figment of his imagination.
The only question of profit or loss that there is in this transaction is as to the price of the first 25,000 tons of rails, that is the only financial question involved ; and the simple question which this committee has to decide is whether the government has been wise in agreeing to give $32.60 per ton, the then going price on the 26th of September or thereabouts, for the purpose of securing the establishment of a steel rail manufactory in the Dominion of Canada. That is the only question. Now, our hon. friends opposite say : In giving $32.60 per ton, you are paying something like $8 per ton more than they were worth at the time you made this contract, you could have bought them at the present time for $8 per ton less than you are paying. That is to say, if we had not made that contract in September, we might have bought the same rails for something like $8 per ton cheaper, but they would not have been Canadian rails, and we would not have had the advantage of securing the establishment of this industry. But, that is not all. We did

not even go the length of giving $8 per ton more for these rails for the purpose of giving assistance to that industry ; we bought the rails at the market price at that time. It has been pointed out elsewhere, by men connected with the trade, that all the government did was to agree to buy
25,000	tons of rails at the then going price, that although the government were aware there was a possibility of a fall in the market, they took the chances and gave $32.60 per ton in order that we might get that industry established. So, as I said, all this committee has to decide is, whether the government was wise, in so far as the financial part of the transaction is concerned, in making that contract at that time, in a market which men in business considered likely to be a falling market, and which ultimately proved to be a falling market. I do not think any member of this committee, giving the matter a reasonable consideration, will think that the government was unwise in giving that much assistance in the purchase of these rails for the purpose of establishing an industry of that kind in Canada. I doubt if any hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, if they will abstain from travelling out of the record and will confine themselves to the actual point at issue, will say that the purchase of these rails at that price for the purpose of securing the establishment of a steel rail factory in Canada, was an uuwise or an improvident transaction.
Now, my hon. friend from Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has made some observations on this question. As a comparatively new member of this House, I always listen with a considerable degree of interest to what he says, and I very often derive considerable information from the remarks which he addresses to the House. But, I am bound to say that the hon. gentleman is not always happy when he undertakes to make an attack upon the government. I do not think he was happy when he made his attack this afternoon. I do not think the hon. gentleman himself would say that it was not a wise or a provident transaction for the government to furnish that amount of assistance for the purpose of getting a steel rail industry established in Canada. He refers to the fact that this transaction took place shortly before the election, and the obvious impression he sought to create in the minds of the committee was, that there was some connection between this transaction and the proximity of the general election. I presume that my hon. friend's experience has led him to that conclusion. But, I would not suggest that there was anything that was not quite proper in connection with his experience. I may remind my hon. friend, however, that there are certain principles in connection with the transaction of public business upon which his mind is much clearer now than when the hon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: gentleman occupied the position of Minister of Railways and Canals ; for instance, the principle of letting public contracts by open tender and public competition.
Give an instance.

What I want, however, to point out is that the suggestion of the hon. gentleman to the effect that this transaction occurred immediately previous to the election, is not founded on fact at all, because the gentlemen who were engaged in connection with the establishment of this magnificent plant, a plant of which I am satisfied every Canadian will be proud, had been discussing these matters with the government for. I think-I speak from memory-nearly twelve months before this contract was made, and if my hon. friends opposite are not satisfied that such is the fact, I will give them absolute proof that the establishment of a steel rail industry in Canada was in contemplation long before that contract was entered into. If my hon. friends will look at the Subsidy Act, introduced by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals last year, if their memory requires that they should do so, and if they will look at section C, they will find this provision :
The Governor General in Council may make it a condition of the subsidies hereby granted, or of any heretofore granted by any Act of parliament as to which a contract has not yet been entered into between Her Majesty and the company for the construction of the railway, that the company shall lay its road with new steel rails made in Canada, if such rails are procurable in Canada of suitable quality upon terms as favourable as other rails can be obtained upon, of which the Minister of Railways and Canals shall be the judge.
When these gentlemen came to discuss with members of the government the question of the establishment of their rail mill, the proposition was that railway companies should be compelled to take their subsidies in steel rails furnished by a Canadian mill if the Canadian mill would supply them at the market price. Subsequently that proposition was modified and we were asked to embody in the Subsidy Act the provision that, under the conditions specified, they should lay their railways with Canadian rails. That was done, and that was the first attempt to carry out the propositions which were made to us for the purpose of assisting and encouraging the establishment of this plant. Then, afterwards, the contract which is under discussion was made. So that, there is nothing at all in the suggestion of the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals that the conduct of this matter was a matter which simply arose immediately before the holding of the general election. This was a matter which had been under consideration, and which had been practically carried to a conclusion months before the submission of the report to coun-

cil of wliicli I have read an extract. Now, I do not wish to detain the committee at any length, but, it is desirable, when we are discussing these matters, to arrive at a proper conclusion upon these questions. The government has entered into a transaction which is said by bon. gentlemen opposite in a very loud tone of voice, and with a great deal of iteration to be an unbusinesslike transaction. Governments are bound to do a great deal of business, and they do that business in the way which they believe to be the most businesslike. The opposition generally seize the opportunity of saying that the transaction in question is unbusinesslike, and it is desirable under such circumstances to find out what independent business men outside of the House think of the transaction which may be under discussion. That is my reason for calling the attention of the committee to an article which will be found in the journal entitled the Canadian Hardware and Metal Merchant, published at Montreal and Toronto, and devoted especially to the hardware and metal trade. Inasmuch as this journal devotes itself particularly to a trade in the line of the transaction we are discussing, its opinion may be received with more authority. This journal goes on to point out, in words from which I will read an extract in a minute or two, that the establishment of a steel rail plant in the Dominion of Canada is an extremely desirable thing. It points out, and this is a point which the committee ought to well consider, that steel rails are upon the free list in Canada, that there is no duty upon steel rails, and that a manufacturer, starting in to manufacture steel rails, is not in the same position as the manufacturer of ordinary commodities, that upon all ordinary commodities there is an average duty of from 25 to 30 per cent, and that upon steel rails there is no duty. Why ? It has been the policy of the Dominion of Canada for many year's that steel rails should be on the free list, because of the desirability of encouraging the construction of railways in Canada, and because of the fact that we did not think our iron and steel industries had arrived at that point at which the manufacture of steel rails could be successfully carried on. In 1888 the Finance Minister of the late government, Sir Charles Tupper, discussed this question in his budget speech and he said then that he had been urged to put a duty on steel rails for the purpose of encouraging the establishment of such an industry, but he pointed out that the time had not come in the history of Canada when such an industry could be successfully established, and. if I recollect rightly, his words were that in ten years from that time the establishment of such an industry might be looked for. If you look at the amount which has been paid by the contract, even looking at it in the most unfavourable way, in excess of
what foreign rails could have been purchased for, it will not amount to more than $8 a ton, which would not be more than about the average rate of duty that is paid upon similar commodities. If there were an average rate of duty upon these rails and if the government were called upon to buy rails, then the government would, in justice to the industry, have to take account of the duty which was placed upon them, so that, looking at it in the most unfavourable way, the government have not done any more than to pay, as the price of the encouragement of the establishment of this industry, the amount of the reasonable duty that would be levied for the assistance or the protection of the manufacturer. Now, I have only to say in conclusion that I desire to call the attention of the committee to the opinion of a business journal upon this transaction. The opinion which is given in the words of the journal itself is as follows :
The action of the government in placing the order in question has caused quite a little adverse criticism. The main points of the contention are : (1) that tenders should have been called for ; (2) that the price paid was higher than that ruling, a decline having taken place a'few days before the contract was signed.
Under ordinary conditions the objections would have been well taken; but they were not ordinary. Mr. Clergue, on behalf of the company that is making such an industrial revolution at Sauit Ste. Marie, Ont., came to the government with a proposition to establish a nickel-steel rail industry:	What he wanted, of course, was
some encouragement from the government. And he got the encouragement in the shape of an order for 25,000 tons of rails at $32.85, delivered at the points named by the government. It was certainly, with the iron and steel market in the condition it was last fall, not the way any ordinary business corporation would have placed a similar order. But the government was desirous of giving some assistance to an industry which we have practically never had, but which we have for a generation been trying to get. There is not an industry in this country that has not, either directly from the Dominion treasury or through a protective tariff, received governmental assistance. And the difference in the market price of steel rails when the 25,000 tons in question are delivered and the price which the government contracted to pay will represent the measure of that assistance. If the government is to be condemned on that score, then must the whole system of protection to home industries be condemned.
This journal concludes by saying :
We have more often condemned than commended the government for its actions, but we do not see in the present instance how we can do any other than commend it.
That is the opinion of a trade journal which is most competent to deal with this question. I think the view of the committee will be, -when its attention is directed to the actual circumstances of the transaction, that the government has shown a desire to encourage the establishment of an

/
industry tliat will do a great deal to promote the prosperity of the Dominion of Canada, and that the attempt which our hon. friends on the other side of the House *are making to misrepresent and distort the facts of the case will entirely fail.

I think the hon. minister (Mr. Sifton) who spoke with so much unction and satisfaction at the words of wisdom contained in that trade journal which he has been quoting, would have done well to have posted himself a little on the question of steel rails. He has repeated more than a dozen times within a quarter of an hour that steel rails are free of duty and he has quoted the trade journal to prove that. I have here a copy of the tariff at present in force and I see that iron and steel railway bars or rails of any form, &c., have a duty of 30 per cent and they are not free at all.
Only for street railways.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

-which term for this purpose shall include all kinds of railways, street railways and tramways.
Therefore the hon. gentleman will have to revise his knowledge of the tariff in that regard. Now, Mr. Chairman, coming to the general question, it appears to me that we are entering upon a new era in this country. We are to have $4,000,000 of the money of the people of Canada exploited without the consent of the people being asked or received. The Minister of Railways on the 9th of April asked the House to pass his estimates which included an item foil $500,000 for steel rails and other things, and the minister explained the transaction in a general way. But, when we came to examine into It we found this simple looking item involved an expenditure by the government of the country of $4,000,000, and the minister expected us to pass it without his giving anything more than a very cursory explanation. Now, the minister tells us that that $4,000,000 is not to be expended at all, and that parliament is only bound to the expenditure for one year. Mr. Chairman, that is a solemn binding contract for $4,000,000 so far as the government of Canada can make a contract and it is as binding for the five years as it is for the first year. The only difference in regard to it is tljat for the first year the price is definitely and precisely fixed, and that wliife for the next four years the price is also definitely and precisely fixed, that price may be variable, as it is to be the price in the English market at the date the order for rails is given by the Minister of Railways. It stands to reason that this company is not going to undertake this industry on the faith of a contract for one year, because if they require assistance or encouragement to go into the enterprise Mr. SIFTON.
they would require it for more than one year. The government have virtually made a contract with them for five years, tvny did not the government submit that to parliament ? Have they the power of their own volition to bind this country for five years ; have they power to make that contract at all without taking the parliament of Canada into their confidence? We are told that these negotiations were in an advanced state in the month of June of last year. Parliament was sitting then, and was parliament informed of the negotiations ? Not a word was whispered outside the sacred precincts of the council chamber. The people of the country did not know. Those who were willing to go into the manufacture of steel rails did not know, and the government took every care not to let them know before the election that they had made the contract. When was the contract made ? Why, the Minister of the Interior with his usual inaccuracy stated that the arrangement was made on the 20th September, and that on that date the price of steed rails was $32.00 a ton. That is not true and he cannot prove it.
I read the order.

The hon. gentleman read the order of the 26th of September. I am not disputing that. But the further statement he mSde and which he cannot prove was that the price of steel rails on that date was $32.00 a ton.
Higher than that, for six weeks after in England.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, I have here the official returns of the monthly summary of the commerce and the finance of the United States, compiled by the Bureau of Statistics of the Treasury Department of the United States. This is a correct official statement. What do they say They say that on the 12tli of September the price of steel rails was $30. Mind you, be says the bargain was made on the 26th. The order in council was passed on the 9th of October. On the 5th of October the price was $26 a ton, according to this official statement.
What was the price on the 26th ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
$26 a ton.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS a'nD CANALS. In the United States ?

In the United States. Where else do you go for the price ? Did you not buy your rails there ? Did you not make both your contracts last year to buy rails from the United States ? Were not the United States sending their rails to England ? Did not the Canadian Pacific I Railway buy 100.000 tons of rails from the

United States tlie year before ? All the transactions of recent years have been with the United States, and this is the official record of the price in the United States. Therefore, the Minister of the Interior misleads this House and tells the House inaccurately that the price on September 26tli, when the contract was made, was $32.60 a ton. He states what he cannot prove because it is contrary to the facts.
What I did was to read the report of the Minister of Railways in which it was stated the price was $32.60. That was the price they were paying at that time.
No. That is what the minister himself said to the House, and he pledged his reputation to this House for a statement that was not true and that he cannot prove is true.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Wallace) is making a statement that is wholly incorrect. I read the report stating it clearly word for word.
(Mr. WALLACE. There is no doubt of what the minister said for I took it down.

Here are the words of the document which I read to the House :
The price to he paid for the said rails so delivered to be fixed upon at $32.60 a ton, which, as above stated, is the price now being paid by the department.
That is what I read.

The Minister of the Interior stated this and I took his words down and ' Hansard ' will show it. He said :
The price current at that date, on the 26th of September, or thereabouts.
That is what he said. But it was not the price at that date. The Minister of Railways and the Minister of Finance tell us, ' Oh. we are not looking at the price on a particular date ; we are not bothering about that.' Why not ? When you are making a bargain involving sucb enormous sums of the money of the people of Canada, why not apply ordinary business acumen to the business in hand ? The Minister of (Finance told us this afternoon, ' We ax-e not in the habit of blazoning contracts through the streets.' When the money of the people of Canada is being squandered, they do not consider that they are bound to give the people any knowledge of what is going on. ' We are not going to tell the people ; we are going to keep our business locked up.' What right have they to do that ? When the smallest contract is let for the erection of a public building or a lighthouse, the next day you see all about it in the papers -the price paid, and the name of the man who receives the contract. What right have they to do differently in this case ?
On the 9th of October they passed that order in council. On the 9th of October another order in council was passed dissolving the House of Commons of Canada, and another one issuing the writs for the general election. It is a curious coincidence that on the same day that parliament was dissolved they passed the order in council giving a contract of that magnitude to Mr. Clergue of the Sault syndicate. Why did they not let the people of Canada know ? What was the object of keeping that a profound secret from the 9th of October to the 9th of April, just six months to a day ? Was there anything to he ashamed of ? Was it something the people of Canada had no right to have a knowledge of ? If that was the case, then, of course, they were right; and these masters, these bosses, these autocrats, who are holding the reins of power to-day, disdained to inform the people of Canada. For six long months they never opened their mouths. Will some one give us the reason why that Important fact was kept from every man in Canada outside the council chamber ? I say it is a scandalous transaction. It is illegal to attempt to make contracts without the consent of parliament. The Minister of the Interior has had a little exjxerience in that line, and perhaps his experience would induce him to avoid asking the consent of the people or the people's representatives. He remembers tlie Yukon Railway and the secret bargain he made with regard to it, almost a day before tbe House met, subject, however, to the consent of parliament in that case. But the parliament of Canada did not consent, and that enormous scheme failed to go through.
The people's representatives consented.
But the great balance-wheel did not consent, and the people of Canada endorsed the course of the Senate of Canada.
No, no.

In that case they tried to get possession of three and three-quarter millions of the best mineral lands in the world at one-tenth of their value. But the government then learned a lesson ; and in this case they said, ' We have got a secret bargain, and we will keep it from the people of Canada.' Why did they not tell the people on the 9th of October, ' We have just concluded a bargain with the Clergue syndicate, and we ask ydur approval or your disapproval.' No ; they were afraid to let it be known-why ? The Minister of Finance quoted a case in which he said tbe bargain was upset because there was a corrupt consideration attached to it. Surely there was not a corrupt consideration in this case. Surely these men were not going to receive a portion of the moneys back again. The

$32.60 a ton was not the whole of the money the syndicate were to get. In addition to that, they are to get $7-$0 from the Dominion, and $1 from the province of Ontario-for every ton of steel rails. That is, $39.60 for an article which was worth $26 a few months ago, and which to-day I am told, is worth $24.85. They say, 'We cannot tell what the price will he in the future.' But I say you have no right in a falling market to go back to the time when steel rails were $35 or $40 a ton ; you are bound to come down to the price on the day the contract was made. They did not do that, because on that day, as the records show, the price of steel rails was just $26 per ton. Now, I say, these gentlemen -have acted illegally in making a contract without the consent of parliament. Year by year we see the powers of parliament taken away by these gentlemen, contracts given without the safeguards which the law provides, and this government snaps its fingers at the law. Here we have the most glaring instance of it. But they say, this year is the only year to consider. So far as the money payment is concerned, it is, Mr. Chairman, I must ask for a little order. Hon. gentlemen opposite look as if they were panic-stricken.
Oh, oh.

I was looking at the uneasy footsteps of the Minister of Customs tramping all over tins House. I would like to know what is disturbing the spirit of his dreams to-night. I was going to say, Mr. Chairman, that our good friend from Algoma (Mr. Dyment) got up to-night and told us that he was up in Sault Ste. Marie, which is in his own constituency, and had the assurance of Mr. Clergue that they were going right along with the construction of this great plant for the manufacture of steel rails. Well, I have the Toronto Globe tonight in my hand, and it gives an entirely different story, and given by Mr. Clergue himself. He tells the correspondent of the Globe :
At present the syndicate is building a plant which will be complete and in operation by September, having a capacity of 600 tons of steel rails per day.
I would like to know where the Minister of Railways and the hon. member for Algoma got their information that these rails would be delivered in August if the shop is not built until September.

What the hon. gentleman Is quoting are the words of Mr. E. D. Clergue, of Michipieoten, who is not in S^ault Ste. Marie possibly four or five times a year. I got mine from Mr. F. H. Clergue, who makes his home there.

Mr. E. D. Clergue apparently knows more about it than the hon. member for Algoma, because he is one of Mr. WALLACB.
the officers of the syndicate conducting the great Sault Ste. Marie enterprise. He was in the city yesterday, and outlined the above project in an interview with the representative of the Globe. Besides, a single pound of pig iron cannot be made by the whole combination at the ' Soo.' They have to go elsewhere for their pig iron. They have not got the pig iron plant, which is the foundation of the business. First you have to make the pig iron and then manufacture it into steel rails.
How will they get the benefit of the bounty if they do not get the pig iron ?

Let me tell the hon. gentleman and his colleagues, because they seem to be sadly in need of information. The syndicate will buy their iron from the blast furnaces of Midland and Hamilton, to which they will send the ore from the mines at Michipieoten. Later on, Mr. Clergue says, they will build their own smelter at the ' Soo,' but at present they have not even commenced to build the smelter for the purpose of manufacturing the pig iron which Is the foundation of the steel rail Industry. The Clergue syndicate have not even commenced to build the smelter, but will have to send their ore down to the city of Hamilton and the city of Midland, and after it is made into pig iron they will bring back the pig iron to the ' Soo,' and make it into steel, and then will travel back again over the same route and deliver it in the city of Montreal. That is a highly economical way of doing business. But the point in it js this, that these men, by their own statement-and they are pretty sanguine men, we are told, perhaps a little too sanguine, according to the Minister of Railways-will mot be ready to turn out a single ton of steel rails until September. How then can they deliver rails in the month of August ?
Another point, and I think it a most important one, is this : 25,000 tons of steel rails, eighty pounds to the yard, will lay 200 miles of railway. Now 200 miles of railway multiplied by 5, will give 1,000 miles of railway that are going to be laid with steel rails within five years. Do the government railways require it ? Not a bit of it. The life of a steel rail is a good deal longer. The government do not require a
1.000	miles of steel rails to be laid within the next five years, and they will have to explain why it is that they have given an order for such a vast quantity. It will be the old story that we knew twenty-five years ago, when the Mackenzie government bought rails years before they were required, and had them piled up until they were rusting and destroyed from want of use. The same thing will occur again, because the government can have no possible use for all these rails. There is no necessity for taking the steel rails, which are to-day good and efficient and have a long
3G13

life before them, and displacing them by laying eighty-pound new rails in their stead. I would like the government to tell us why they are doing that ?
There is another point. The Minister of Railways tells us that he is not going to supervise all those contracts. He says that he has hundreds and thousands of contracts coining before him and he is not going to supervise them. The government tell us that the party of the other part always signs the contract first and then it is sent back to be signed by the government, which is all right, I presume, but before that contract is sent out is when it should have complete supervision. When you ask a contractor to sign an agreement, he ought to have the certainty that it was carefully considered and that the government intend to abide by it. But the Minister of Railways tells us that he has not signed the contract and that he supposed at first that he had signed it. It was only when it was laid on the Table that he discovered it was not signed. Thereupon the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Clifford Sifton) gets up mid says there is no contract at all. But, I presume that every member of the government was under the impression that that contract, based upon the order in council which they had pasesd upon and agreed to on that celebrated day of the 9th of October, was completed. I venture to say that before the 10th of October there was not a minister who was not under the impression that that contract was completed. But there is something more' behind this and it is a very important consideration. Does any hon. gentleman think that Mr. Clergue made a bargain on the 9th of October and had the order in council in his hand on the 12th of October, and then allowed six months to elapse without offering his signature to it ? Of course, we have to take the statement of the hon. gentleman, but if so what kind of a business government have we got ? Just imagine, here is a contract jmade six months ago, it is lying in Mr. Clergue's desk unsigned by him or the government, the government is not aware that it is not signed, the Minister of Railways is not aware that it is unsigned. He was not aware, when he placed it on the Table of the House, that it was unsigned. They say that it was a mistake to put it there. I presume it was, as they view it. But, the people of Canada want that contract there, they want the particulars, they want to know all about it, and they are entitled to know. But there is something mysterious about it all. Do hon. gentlemen opposite tell us that for six long months nothing was done, that not a word was breathed throughout the country, that nobody knew that Mr. Clergue was building large works for the manufacture of steel rails ? But now, we hear, on the 23rd of April, that they are putting up enormous works where they can manufacture GOO tons
of steel rails in a day, and later will have works that will turn out 2,000 tons per day. If you imagine that Mr. Clergue does business in that way, I think you are mistaken. And, if the government of Canada do their business in that way, I think it is time that we had a new government, and, apparently it will not be long until we get it. I repeat the question : When the government made a contract with Mr. Clergue, whether for one or five years I do not care, why did they not tell the people of Canada that a new era had dawned, that we were undertaking the great enterprise of malting steel rails for the supply of our railroads, beginning with the government railroads, and that a bargain had been made with Mr. Clergue, subject to the sanction and ratification of parliament r These things were not done, and to my mind the government is to be condemned for their secrecy, for their want of business arrangements, for their improvident bargain, and for doing what the law does not permit them to doA making the contract without the consent of parliament.

My hon. friend says he is very much disturbed, aud, apparently he is, by the fact that the contract was made on the 9th of October

I think that was the date he gave. But, I think, from certain references which ran through the hon. gentleman's speech, it will be evident that what has disturbed him is not what took place on the 9th of October, but what took place on the 7th of November. Now, he undertook to call attention to what he called my inaccuracy. I have no objection to being lectured about being inaccurate by any gentleman who is competent to do so, or even by one who endeavours to maintain even the most distant connection between accuracy and his own statement. But, when a gentleman who has been Controller of Customs, who has been, to all intents and purposes, Minister of Customs, and who undertakes to declare the Conservative policy with regard to tariffs, endeavours to give this committee the impression that there is a duty of 30 per cent on steel rails, I object to being lectured by him. If i were to make a statement so inaccurate as that, I would walk out of this room and hide my diminished head. The hon. gentleman is not a new member, he is not a tyro in politics, but a man who professes to be able to teach members of this House finance and tariff legislation. To support his statement he deliberately reads from an item which he knows refers to an entirely different matter :
Iron and steel railway bars or rails of any form, punched or not, n.e.s.-
Every member knows what ' n.e.s' means. I think even the hon. gentleman knows.
Oh, no.

Yes, I think he does. It means ' not elsewhere specified.' And there is a duty of 30 per cent on these goods. What is elsewhere specified ? I turn to schedule B,
* free goods,' and I find :
Steel rails weighing not less than forty-five pounds per lineal yard.
And the rails of which we have been speaking, as my hon. friend must have heard if he listened, are 80 pounds to the yard-and they are free.
I read this item as it was here, as it struck me at the moment

But, the hon. gentleman did not know anything about it.
Mr. WALLACE-as it struck me at the moment while the hon. gentleman was making his remarks. I turned up the item, iron and steel, &c., for railways, 30 per cent. But, I see that other rails are on the free list, and I am not persisting in an inaccuracy like the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Sifton).
The hon. gentleman accuses me of being inaccurate, and yet, though an ex-Coutroller of Customs, did not know what was in the tariff.
That does not excuse the hon. gentleman. He will have to explain his own inaccuracy.

The hon. gentleman says that he did not know, and the assumption on our part that he did not know is the most charitable construction we can put upon his statement, because if he did know he was deliberately misleading the House.

tect and develop home industries; hut we certainly feel that in giving a bounty of $0 a ton to the manufacturers of steel rails, they have gone quite as far as it is necessary to do. and they might have conserved the public interest better if they had limited the contract to the price at which they could have bought the rails in the United States, and still have acted equitably in this matter.
Now the Minister of the Interior, in defence of the action of the government, pleads that this contract is simply for one year and not for five years. That is a point upon which there may be room for difference of opinion ; but I am afraid, judging from the course of the government in the matter, that we cannot expect them to act much more providently the next year than they have done this year. If the government of Canada has put in that contract a condition that the price to be paid for future years shall be the price in England, what is there to justify us in expecting that they will not in succeeding years pay $6, or $7, or $8 a ton more than the market price in the country in which these rails are cheapest, as they have done this year, now that rails are $26 in the United States and they give $32.60, pleading as an excuse that the current price in England at the time when they made the contract was $32.60 a ton ? What is to prevent them, if they wish to do so, finding a similar condition of affairs in England next year ? There can only be one proper, safe or secure position for the government to take, and that would be, if they were going to purchase these rails, to purchase them in the open market, and to consider that the Clergue syndicate was amply protected and amply bonused by the fact that the department was giviug them a contract for 25,000 tons of rails extending over a period of five years during the whole of which these bounties would be paid for, although on a gradually declining scale.
Now, I think one very serious objection to this contract, and one that lias been pointed out over and over again, is the fact that in this agreement, as entered into with the Clergue syndicate for the purpose of developing the manufacture of steel rails in Canada, there is not one line, or one word, which will compel the Clergue syndicate to supply to the government rails either made in Canada, or produced from steel made in Canada. This is certainly a most amazing piece of carelessness, of criminal carelessness, I might almost call it, on the part of the hon. minister who is responsible for the drafting of the instrument. It is perfectly idle for the minister to come to this House with a transaction of such immense proportions involving such an enormous amount of money and set up the defence that some subordinate official in his department has badly drafted the agreement. These subordinate officials are Mr. BELL (Pictou).
not present in this House. They are not responsible to parliament. There is one man and one man only who is responsible to parliament and to the people of Canada, for the blunder, for the carelessness, for the amazing ignorance that is being displayed in this matter by the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals. It is idle, it is useless, it is to subvert every sound principle of parliamentary government to allow the minister to set up such a contention in defence of his conduct. If this syndicate were disposed and were not ready, as they are not ready, to produce steel rails, they can go to the market of the United States, import steel billots and roll these billets into rails in Canada. They can buy steel billets for $18 or $19 a ton, bring them into Canada and at a comparatively small cost, at a cost of some $5 or $6 a ton, they can roll these billets into steel rails. There is nothing in the contract to prevent them (tendering to the government steel rails thus manufactured, and there is nothing in the contract to enable the government to refuse to accept such rails if tendered to them-not one word in the contract that I can discover. I believe that the government has very seldom occupied a more indefensible position than the government occupies in respect to this matter. If it were its purpose to extend a helping hand to the steel rail industry of Canada, why did it proceed in secret ? Why did lion, gentlemen select as their favourites in this matter this particular syndicate which is not in a position to produce one pound of pig iron, and which has not a single steel furnace or rolling mill in operation ? Why did not they open their arms to the manufacturers of steel and iron throughout Canada in every part of this country, so that the advantage of such an immensely important institution as a great steel rail plant would be available to them ? Why was this secrecy observed ? What was the purpose of it ? It seems to me that so far as my own province of Nova Scotia is concerned, the province in which iron development is going on at a rapid rate, it has been most unfairly dealt with by the government in this matter. Why should" they proceed to the eastern end of Lake Superior to attempt to procure rails for a railway commencing at Montreal and ending at Sydney, to the entire exclusion of an industry that produces its own steel, which has the financial resources necessary to establish rolling mills, and which is located at one extremity of that road ? If these rails are to be used, why does the government go to the extreme western end of the province of Ontario ? Taking all these things into consideration, taking into consideration the manner in which they made known to the people of Kingston, without any secrecy whatever, *the fact that they were going to be in a position to turn out locomotives, taking into consideration the secrecy they exhibited in

the matter of the production of steel rails, taking into consideration the fact that the government, just on the eve of an election, entered into a contract involving $4,000,000, there is ground to warrant the suspicion that there was a rake off on a scale of the most gigantic magnitude. Now, the government would not naturally lay itself open to such a suspicion for no purpose whatever, but what else can explain the manner in which the government has proceeded to conduct this whole matter ? Why did the government proceed in secrecy from the moment that it began this negotiation in council with Mr. Olergue, through every step through which this matter has proceeded, in parliament up to this afternoon, when, now, for the first time, parliament is beginning to know the facts of the case? Why should parliament be kept in the dark? Why should these things be kept secret? It is not good government. It is not treating the people with proper respect. It is not treating the representatives of the people with proper respect. It seems to me that the government should not enter into a contract, such as has been entered into, not only for one year, but, involving the policy of the government for five years, during which that government may possibly pass out of power, and leave to their successors a contract, the responsibility of which that succeeding government might not care to take. I say again that in this matter the government is departing from the soundest principles of parliamentary, representative government for no reason whatever that I can see, unless it be for some such improper purpose as may very well be puggested. This most improper contract, involving such huge profits for the syndicate selected, without any reason that any one can discover, to be the favourite of the government, has been entered into. Unless some such improper reason as has been suggested was in existence, it is impossible for any one to discover any reason whatever that should induce the government to conduct this business in the manner in which it has been conducted. To my mind nothing much more wide of the mark than the very amazing statement made by the hon. Minister of the Interior could be conceived. It was a piece of oratory that to my mind was very much more adapted to the stump than to the floor of parliament, designed to divert the attention of parliament and of the country from the facts of the case and to accuse the opposition in this manner, not of finding fault with the government for making this contract, but of finding fault with it for not making it. Now, it may be that history is going to repeat itself. Those men who took part in the campaign of 1878 will recollect that for a much smaller steel rail business the late Hon. Alex. Mackenzie and the government of which he was the leader, received great blame, were held to account, 114}
were passed upon in judgment, and were turned down by the people. This transaction, in whicli this government is involved, is worse than the transaction in which Mr. Mackenzie involved himself. It is greater in extent, it is just as improvident, because this government has committed what is worse than a crime ; it has committed a great blunder. At a time when the market was falling steadily it agreed to purchase steel rails in quantities sufficient to relay 900 miles of Intercolonial Railway, to relay an extent of the system which does not seem to be requisite, according to the figures that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has laid before parliament. The government is committed to the purchase for five years of a sufficient quantity of rails to relay 900 miles of the Intercolonial Railway, showing the most utter incapacity on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite from a business point of view. It is not necessary to say that a private individual would not conduct great business affairs in the manner in which this transaction has been carried out by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals.
It is quite true that the resources of Canada are very great and that our country can bear heavy burdens, but it is not right that we should ask our country to bear such burdens. We have money in abundance and the people of Canada are ready to spend that money in abundance for every legitimate enterprise, but there are thousands of crying wants of this country which the government did not supply and cannot supply, simply because they have not the means. Great as has been their expenditure and many as are the wants they have supplied, they know there are thousands of cases in which the country is calling to them for an outlay which would in all probability bring in a return. Great and strong as Canada is financially, there is no excuse for the administration entering on a transaction of this kind which involves such a great loss of money to the country. So far as the secrecy of the transaction, the disregard of the interests of the people and the disregard of that courtesy due to parliament are concerned, it seems to me that no speaker on the government side has set up anything like an adequate defence for the course which the government in this respect has seen fit to follow.

I wish to ask the
minister : To what account were the steel rails which were taken up on the Intercolonial credited ? I want the minister to be correct and exact in the answer.
Has the hon. gentleman any other question ?
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Yes. I would like to ask the amount of new rails which have been laid on the Intercolonial Railway of

eighty pounds weight, and how many miles the minister intends to relay with them.
I will endeavour to answer the hon. gentleman. Let me say with reference to the matter of the accounts, that I have not been keeping the accounts at Moncton.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Surely, in an important matter like that the deputy minister could tell at once.
I will find out and let the hon. gentleman know accurately.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: While the minister is taking a note, I would like to ask him if it is understood we will have the proposal made by Mr. Clergue which initiated this transaction. There were telegrams also referred to by the minister.
The deputy minister has a note of these things.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In view of the nature of the difficulty which has arisen on this contract, I would like to ask the minister if he will lay on the Table the original contract sent to Mr. Clergue and which no doubt has been returned ?
The hon. gentleman has seen the paper.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: As a difficulty lias arisen as to the extent and the importance of that document, I think it is fair for us to ask that the original draft be laid on the Table of the House.

I have followed the hon. member from Pictou (Mr. Bell) very closely and as a struggling minister endeavouring to master as well as I can the laborious work which devolves upon me in my department, I cannot help but feel how priceless it would be if I possessed the prescience and the intellect and the capacity of the hon. gentleman.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Hear, hear.
You never will.
I never can.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That's right.

I abandon all pretense at foreseeing the rate at which steel rails are to be sold in the market three months, or two months, or one month, or one week hence. I abandon the pretense of knowing whether rails are going to rise or to fall, or of discharging a great many of the other duties which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell, Pictou) would ask me to assume. I recognize that Mr. HAGGART.
the hon. gentleman is a very competent critic and perhaps the hon. gentleman might devote himself to an endeavour to reconcile the views which he has presented with the view which some of his friends have presented, because they appear now to be totally irreconcilable. The first and the most important thing for gentlemen opposite to do is to agree amongst themselves not to make criticisms upon this transaction which are self-destructive. From a party point of view, that is not a wise policy of theirs, and yet the party point of view appears to be the only object which they hope to attain. My hon. friend (Mr. Bell, Pictou) has devoted a good deal of his attention to complaining of the secrecy of this transaction. Can he tell me in what this secrecy has consisted ? Does he complain, as his friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) did complain, that the government did not tell parliament that negotiations were going on 1 Did any one ever hear of a government telling parliament that certain proposals had been made to them, before the government had an opportunity of forming a conclusion upon these proposals ? If the secrecy consists in that, then we have been guilty of secrecy and we have done what every government that ever existed has done, and we have done what every government that ever will exist will do. If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bell) means that we have been guilty of secrecy because no member of the government mentioned this publicly after it was entered upon, then his charge is not correct. The Postmaster General made it a boast on the public platform that the government had made an arrangement with the Lake Superior Company that they should establish a rolling mill, and that they should manufacture rails for the Intercolonial Railway. I did not hear the Postmaster General myself, but I am credibly informed that he stated it publicly on more than one occasion. However, if the Postmaster General did not state it, I stated it more than once, in the course of the speeches I made during the late campaign. After this matter was closed, I told the people that the government, deeming it was necessary that the Intercolonial Railway should be relaid with heavier rails, had availed ourselves of the necessity of doing this for the purpose of encouraging the establishment of an industry which would confer great benefits on the country if it were successful, and which would save the Canadian government and the Canadian people a large amount of money in the expenditure which they made annually for rails. I made that statement not only once, but several times, and the newspaper press reported it. I made it not far from Pictou county. I stated it in Cumberland county, and the hon. gentleman (Mr. Logan) heard me, if I am not mistaken. I stated it in my own county ; I made no secret of it. There was nothing to conceal about it. We were proud as a government

that we were able to take a step which would establish this industry. There was nothing whatever to conceal about it. It was a subject of boast, at all events so far as I was concerned, and I believe so far as other members of the government are concerned. So that, if the hon. gentleman means to say that we are open to serious criticism and censure because we did not speak of this matter publicly, we are not open to the charge, because it was spoken of publicly. The newspaper press mentioned it, and it must have come under the notice of many hon. gentlemen opposite. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) says it was an outrage to buy rails on a falling market. Who bought rails on a falling market ? We did not. The rails we bought were bought at a time when the price in England was as high within five shillings as it had been at 'any time for a year previous or more, and when the price was maintained for weeks afterwards. You cannot tell whether the price of rails or any other article of commerce is going to rise or fall. It is a mere matter of judgment. One man's judgment may be as good as another's. The government, I suppose, are not endowed with any greater capacity of judgment than the same number of men of equal business capacity, and we could not form any better opinion than anybody else on that question. But, we came to the conclusion, from the facts before us, that we were justified, under all the circumstances, in engaging to give this company the price we stipulated for, with the view of establishing that industry in Canada, and thereby ensuring the supply of our steel rails from Canadian sources.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman permit me to ask him a question ?
Certainly.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the government did not buy steel rails on a falling market, but bought them at a period when they were within five shillings of the highest price paid in the English market ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: A good time to make a contract for $4,000,000 of rails, was it not ?

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: May I ask the hon. minister if the government has bought rails since this contract has been made, upon the probability, the certainty to-day, that there will be no rails from the Clergue syndicate to carry out this summer's work ?
No ; and I can tell the hon. gentleman that he could not go into the market to-day and purchase rails for delivery before next year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
May I ask the government, then, if they intend to abandon this year's
work, if the statement made several times

in this House is true, that Mr. Clergue cannot deliver any rails for this summer's work ?

The statement has not been made by any. person who can speak with confidence, as I have followed the discussion, that the Lake Superior Power Company will not be able to carry out their contract with the government. There have been assertions on the other side of the House that they will not; there have been doubts expressed by myself as to whether or not Mr. Clergue will be able to realize his expectations, though I sincerely hope I may be wrong. But, if we do not get the rails from Mr. Clergue, as we hope to get
them,	we are not going to get them anywhere else. We are not going to be in such a great hurry to secure these rails that we are going to hurt this undertaking, i think the government will be justified in treating the Lake Superior Power Company in a spirit of fairness, and in encouraging them as far as we can legitimately do so without deteriment to the public interest. That is how I feel about it personally, and in that I am speaking for nobody but myself.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
May I ask the hon. minister,
then,	is it a fact that the government do not require the rails ?

We do require them. They ought to be put down as rapidly as possible ; and I may meet that question now. The question is asked, why do you propose to take 25.000 tons of rails per year for these five years, and what is the need of laying them on the Intercolonial Railway ? The policy of the government is this. It is to put the Intercolonial Railway upon a proper business footing, and that requires it to be relaid from end to end with heavy steel rails. It is not now so laid.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: How heavy are the present rails ?

With the exception of those put down last year, all those that were laid before we took over the Drummond County Railway, which has a seventy-pound rail, are only C.7 pounds in weight, and we are putting from 80 to 00-ton engines upon that road, and the sooner we get our line relaid with heavy rails, the better it wrill be for the Intercolonial Railway and the country. The sooner we get heavy locomotives upon our line and heavy rails, the quicker will we realize the advantages which will follow. If we have a supply of 25.000 tons per year for five or six years, we will be able to relay the main line of the Intercolonial Railway from end to end. We have been going on from time to time putting down heavy rails in the last year or Mr. MONK.
two, but we have not done the work as rapidly as we should, but when an opportunity of this kind presented itself, when the proposal was made to us by responsible parties that they were about establishing a rail making industry in Canada-a thing which has been much desired for many years past-we thought that we were carrying out a well considered policy in contracting for steel rails, and at the same time establishing a most important industry in the country, which otherwise in all probability would not be established. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) wants to know why we picked out this one company and extended favour to it ? In the first place we did not pick them out, they came to us. I had not the faintest idea that for some years there would be the probability of such an industry as this being established in Canada. When Mr. Clergue came to us, having done as much as he had, having achieved so successful results, and having, as we believed, ample capital for the purpose, we felt that here was an opportunity which might not occur again for many a day, and that it was our duty to make satisfactory terms to encourage this company in proceeding with its undertaking. We considered their proposals carefully and adopted them to the extent we have stated to the committee. We have not, therefore, treated this matter in any secret or unusual way, but have just done what hon. gentlemen would have condemned us for not doing, if we had failed to avail ourselves of our opportunity. There is not an hon. member who has followed the discussion who is not confident that if the proposal of Mr. Clergue, embodied in our order in council, had been turned down -there is not a man in this House who does not believe that in such a case the same gentlemen who criticise and condemn us, because we are making a progressive movement would not have condemned us if we had not availed ourselves of this arrangement.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
in that government, and they would have pointed to the order in council and the written contract and would have said : If you are worthy representatives of Her Majesty in government, you will carry out the obligation we have entered into with Mr. Clergue for $4,000,000. That is what they would have said, and that is what the people of Canada would have understood by such an arrangement. Has the time arrived wheu a contract can be made with the government and they, at their own will, can say to the contractor : It is true that you have an order in council which we have asked the representative of His Majesty to sign, you have a contract, but it is only a moral obligation and not worth the paper it is written on. Mr. Chairman, I do not believe that either the courts of the land or the great moral sentiment of the people of Canada, if appealed to, would support or endorse the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite on this occasion. The hon. gentleman said that steel rails to-day could not be bought for less than he is paying. It is well known that you can buy steel rails delivered in Montreal for $26 a ton. This is no fable, this is no midsummer night's dream, it is a fact-you can buy as many tons as you choose to order at that price. I do not understand the hon. gentleman's objection to going to the United States for these rails. He has gone there for cars, he has gone there for engines, why should he not go there for steel rails ? He has got from the United States everything that is necessary for the supply of the Intercolonial Railway, why should he make an exception with steel rails ? Why ? It is to adopt the grand principle of protection, to show to the native industries of Canada, to the miners of the iron ore that has Iain so long the hidden treasure of Canada, to say to the people of Canada : In us you see the copyists of the government that have gone before ; we ask for your favour because we are doing those things that the government who went before us did better than we know how to do.
Well. Sir, it is amusing, it is interesting, to see the Minister of Railways and Canals appeal to his deputy. I could not help but think of the appeals that had been made'upon more than one occasion, for the benefit of the statements made by the minister, to that deputy, a gentleman who stands in point of integrity even the equal of the minister who makes a moral contract in this country only for $4,000,000. Why, Sir, he made me think of an old gentleman in our part of the country who was never known to tell the truth. He had a wife whose name was Sophia, and whenever he made a statement that was criticised, or if any objection was taken to it, he would say : ' If you do not believe me, if you do not want to take my word, ask Sophia.' And when I heard the minister appealing to his deputy, that venerable deputy, who has passed through so many governments, and saw him bowing Mr. POPE.
his head and heard him whispering his consent, I thought of the old man who appealed to Sophia. Sir, I may be mistaken, I may not know how to appreciate a moral obligation on the part of this government, a government who have not, so far as I know, kept any single obligation that they ever promised to keep since they came into power. It is hard, Mr. Chairman-and, by the way, I see we have a new chairman. I can understand that also, I can understand that the trying circumstances in which a man is placed who holds the impartial position of a chairman, listening to the contradictory arguments of hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House, it is necessary for the restoration of health of the chairman, that he should retire and be replaced from time to time. Vigorous as this present chairman seems to be, I have no doubt that we shall have another one before this debate is over. I do not think that nature has given him strength enough to withstand the electrical inconsistencies that will shock him as they pass from the other side of the House during this debate.
Now, Sir, the minister has stated to us that there is great necessity, urgent necessity, that he should have these steel rails, so great that he had to make this contract just before they appeal to the electorate. He has also stated this afternoon that he has made this contract with rhe company, and lie does not know if it is possible for them to carry it out. Why all this haste ? Why all this urgency previous to the general election ? Now, Sir, if the hon. minister had not a reputation through Canada, if he had not made a reputation for himself in his native province before he ever came to this House, perhaps he could escape. But, knowing, as he must know, how the people of Canada view him, coupled with the Minister of Public Works-for the people look upon that pair of gentlemen as the two great pushers of the government upon certain occasions. Now, it is not for me to say if that is true. I have never been consulted by the Prime Minister or by either of those two hon. gentlemen, but public opinion says that they are the two gentlemen who provide the weapons of war, public opinion says that they distributed a million and a half dollars among the electorate of Canada during the last election on behalf of lion, gentlemen on the other side of the House. Sir, could this have been connected with steel rails ? Is it possible there is any association between that election and steel rails ? Or, was it to fulfil a moral obligation on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite with the electorate of this country ? Did they carry out that moral obligation, or is it like all their other contracts, not worth the paper that it was written upon ? Sir, I remember a moral obligation entered into in the city of Sherbrooke previous to the last general election. I discovered there the track of steel rails. I remember perfectly the offer that was
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Blair) has not given me the information that I asked him for.
I will give the hon. gentleman the statement now. The rails taken up have been put in store and have been credited to the new rails' account.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well, we have the statement from the hon. gentleman that they have been put in store and credited to the new rails' account. If this is so, what does the hon. gentleman want with $920,000 ?
That is a statement I made to the hon. gentleman, I think, last week.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Tlie statement that the hon. gentleman made last week was that the whole of the rails were charged to capital account.
Less the old rails.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. gentleman did not say anything about less the old rails, and I will not be certain that the minister is correct at the present moment. If he credits the old rails to -the account of the new rails, why does he aslc for $920,000 ?
I am not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman asked for $420,000 last year and he asks for $500,000 this year. I asked him to give me the amount of road that he is to relay but the hon. gentleman did not seem to know. According to the last report of the chief engineer of his department, there is 1,315 miles on the Intercolonial Railway. From Montreal to Halifax there are 840 miles, from Moncton to St. John eighty-nine miles, from Truro to Sydney, 217 miles, the North Sydney branch, five miles, or 1,170 miles, with 274 miles of sidings. I suppose that the hon. gentleman has laid the whole length of the Drummond County Railway, about eighty miles, with 80-pound rails, and he has laid about thirty miles more of the road, I should judge from the statement of his chief engineer, with 80-pound rails. There is the whole of the Drummond county section laid, and there are thirty miles of another portion of the Intercolonial Railway. That leaves 1,075 miles of the Intercolonial Railway to be laid with 80-pound steel rails. The hon. gentleman very correctly stated that nearly the whole of the road, with the exception of about 118 miles, has been relaid with 67-pound rails, that the old 57-pound rails have been taken up and G7-pound rails substituted in their place. Then, for the 1,075 miles it would require 125 tons to the mile, or altogether 134,375 tons of rails, and I am adding about three tons per mile for rail fastenings and such things. The increased weight of fish-plates and bolts between the 57 and 67-pound rails would represent an increased weight of twenty-one tons per mile, and the increased weight between the 67 and 80-pound rail, including plates and bolts, is about twenty-eight tons per mile. The total increased weight, therefore, would only be, for 1,075 miles, 33,040 tons. Now, the hon. gentleman credits the old rails that he takes off the Intercolonial Railway to the account of the new rails, and is required to provide, in order to relay his whole road, for the price of 33,040 tons of rail. At the price he is paying to the syndicate, $32.60 per ton, he has. with the vote he got last year and with the vote he gets this year, got more than enough to relay the whole Intercolonial Railway with Mr. BLAIR.
an 80-pound steel rail. As for the statement that his deputy minister gives him, and the statement that he made to the committee that the old rails which were taken off the Intercolonial Railway are credited to the account of the rails which are being placed upon the road, the only amount that he requires is the difference between the price of the old and the new rails. I doubt very much if this statement is correct, and I would like the hon. minister to be accurate and give me the information to-morrow, because this item cannot go through to-night without the fullest possible information on the subject. I wish to know whether the rails taken off the road are not credited to the revenue or receipts on the Intercolonial Railway, as they have been in the past ?
Never.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: They were. When I was Minister of Railways, all the rails that went on the road were charged to the ordinary revenue, and the old rails were deducted from the cost of the new. I asked the minister the other ddy what became of the old rails, and I was astonished to hear him say that they went into store account. I asked him tq be certain as to what account the new rails were charged, and after consulting his deputy, he said that every rail that went on that road, was charged to capital account.
Less the old rails.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The minister did not say that.
I think so.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why does he ask for $500,000 this year, and why did he ask for $420,000 last year if it be correct that the cost of the old rails is deducted from the cost of the new. He should only have the difference between the cost of the old rails and the cost of the new rails. Instead of that he asks for more than the full amount necessary to purchase new rails, and I venture to say the total cost without any deduction for the old rails will be charged to capital. However, I want to be certain and I want to know how the new rails are charged. We want to-morrow the contract as originally entered into, that was sent to Mr. Clergue for the purpose of signing. This document that was laid on the Table purporting to be the contract, has a memorandum at the bottom of it which I did not notice at first. ,
It was there. It was handed to the hon. gentleman just as he has it now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I did not notice the certificate of Mr. Schreiber on it as I first saw it.
It was there.
speakername: The MINISTER OE RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I may be misinformed, but at all events, it commences ' This indenture,' and purports to be signed by the Minister of Railways and the clerk of the department. He says he did not sign it, that he sent it to Mr. Clergue to sign it first, and that he even did not see the contract. It is a most extraordinary position. In the first place the minister stated to the House that he made a contract only for 25,000 tons, which he told us was at the lowest market price, and he said he 'made it in order to develop the steel industry.
