When we got the contract we found it was for 125,000 tons of steel rails, and the contract in no way goes past the memorandum which the minister sent for the assent of the Governor General and his colleagues. In fact it is not only for 125,000 tons, but for 150.000 tons of rails. The first 125,000 tons is to be delivered, and it enables him to enter into a contract for five successive years for 25,000 tons each year, making in all 150,000 tons. That question will be debated later, and I shall not do more now than remark on the extraordinary contentions made by the Minister of the Interior and the Minister of Finance. The Minister of the Interior denied that the government was not bound to take delivery of 125,000 tons, but the Minister of Finance made the extraordinary statement that there was only a moral obligation ; that the successors of this government would not be bound by it, but he evidently has abandoned that position since. What is the use of quibbling about the legality of it. The Minister of Railways says that he will carry out the contract. And although the Minister of Finance says that they are morally bound, though not legally bound, the Minister of the Interior, more careful than the others, admits the liability under the order in council which is signed by the Governor General, and admits that the party interested can enforce his rights as set forth in the order in council. It is absurd to state that Mr. Clergue has raised 810.000,000 for the purpose of starting an industry at Sault Ste. Marie on a mere moral obligation. He goes with the order in council to financiers who are accustomed to deal with governments, and who know that most governments in the world keep their word, not to speak of the strict legality of it. On that contract Mr. Clergue raises his money. Every member of the government, and every member of the House intends to carry out" to the best of their ability the. words which they put in the order, which they asked His Excellency to sign. The Minister of Railways boasts that he has started an industry in this country, and he challenges us to know if we would not do the same thing. He said
he announced it to the people in New Brunswick, but it is strange that an important contract involving $4,000,000 was never heard of in the public press in this country. The member for Algoma (Mr. Dyment) says that the Postmaster General made the statement in Algoma. Perhaps he did but if he did he made it in a locality where it never reached the press. No one in this country of any importance ^except the parties interested ever heard of this contract. Not one member of this House ever heard of it. That is a nice position for a political party to be in, whose platform used to be that all public contracts should contain a clause that they would be submitted to parliament. I have heard Mr. Blake again and again contend in this House that all these contracts should be put on the Table within five days of the meeting of the House. But there was not a word about this contract from the government. They were ashamed of it. I venture to say that even the colleagues of the Minister of Railways did not know the extent of this contract until it was discussed in this House the other day. I will venture to say that he led them to believe that it was only a contract for 25,000 tons of rails, and that they were amazed to find that they had entered into a contract for 125,000 tons of rails which the Intercolonial Railway does not require. But the bon. gentleman is going to make the old road hum. He is going to put it in a position which it never occupied before. When we come to discuss the railway, we shall wish to see where it is today from the back to the front. Instead of being a local road, the hon. gentleman was going to make it a great trunk line, carrying its proportion of freight along with the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway. We shall see whether it is carrying any more through freight to-day than it was in 1896. However, perhaps I am diverging to a subject which may be discussed at a future stage ; but this may serve as a warning to the minister that there will be a discussion on that point.
Do not frighten me.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I suppose not. Nothing could frighten the hon. gentleman. There was something, however, which frightened him the other day, when his colleagues discovered the contract they had entered into. Between that and something else the hon. gentleman was not here for several days.
That is not a very fair remark for the hon. member to make.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I do not know the unfairness of the remark. I do not know that the hon. gentleman was unwell or that

he had any other reason for his little outing. But we shall have a full discussion of the matter on another occasion, and the point I want to make at the present time is that we wish to have full information in this matter-the contract, the proposals made hy Mr. Clergue, the telegram, the original contract that was sent to him, a statement of the number of 80-pound rails which are being laid, the number which have been laid out of those for which $420,000 was voted, the rails which are unlaid, and the number he proposes to lay with the $500,000. We shall then have the full information, and be in a position to discuss the matter intelligently. But the hon. minister must not expect us without this full information to pass the item; and as it is now near twelve o'clock, perhaps he had better let it stand till the next meeting, and when we get that information, we will discuss it as briefly as possible.
Mr. SPROUT,E. I want to say a few words on the secrecy of this contract. If it was for the purpose of establishing a new steel industry in the country, one would naturally suppose that if would be popular, and therefore it would be a matter of importance that it should be given to the world at the earliest possible moment. We find that this contract was entered into on the 9th of October, the same day on which parliament was dissolved and on which the order was passed for the issue of the writs, so that on that day the government was practically a defunct government. They were appealing to the country, and they might have expected that possibly they would not be returned with a majority at their back, and they would be leaving a legacy to their successors which might have turned out to be very embarrassing to them. The question arises, why was there such secrecy about this contract ? The Postmaster General was up in our country and talked on platform after platform, and I know that he used the influence of the Clergue company to assist him in the election. I know -that the moral influence of that company was at the back of the government. It was something that could not be understood at the time-the new-born zeal of the Clergue company for the present government. Now we are told that the information was given to the world somewhere back an Algoma ; but why was that not done when the Postmaster General spoke at Mea-ford and suggested that the board of trade invite Mr. Clergue down to see the place, and give him a banquet ? Why was it not done at the time he advised| the people of Meaford to bring Mr. Clergue down and get him on the platform to assist the government in the election of their candidate against myself ? Why was it not done when the Postmaster General spoke at Feversham, in the township of Osprey, or in the county of Si-mcoe ? If it was a good bargain and likely to be popular with Mr. HAGGART
the country, they would have given it to the world at once ; but the secrecy about it justifies the suspicion that the transaction was a colourable one. Up there it was currently believed that the government got a large subscription from this company. There was no doubt they did their best in a quiet way to help the government in the election. We did not understand it then, but we understand it now. What was the reason -they did not give the matter to the world, and enable us to discuss it wisely and intelligently ? Was it a proper reason -I do not think it was-why the people were kept in the dark with reference to this transaction, which took place on the very day the House was dissolved and the writs were issued for a new election, and the very day the government praotieally ceased to be a government ?

I may mention that there will not be the slightest objection to bring down the information which the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) desires ; and if be wishes at the same time that the matter be not further proceeded with now, I have not the slightest objection, as it is near twelve o'clock. But, let me say a word In answer to my bon. friend,who is much concerned about this question of secrecy, and the marvellous coincidence that this order in council was passed exactly on the day the order in council dissolving parliament was passed. The hon. gentleman has some little public experience, and he knows, in the first place, from the papers which have been produced and read, that this matter was practically-settled in August. He knows that on account of my absence the report of council did not come in until September, and he knows that it is an exceedingly difficult tiling to get any meeting of council at such a time as that, when my hon. friend and all his associates were passing through the country arousing the electors ; and I apprehend that members of the government were out pretty much on the same business. It was not easy to get a meeting of council. I was not present at this one myself, and I do believe that there was none for some time previously. A meeting of council was held of necessity for that purpose, and for any other business that required to be disposed of.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: If the Lake Superior Power Company are unable to manufacture steel rails at the ' Soo ' this year, and should purchase rails manufactured in England and the United States, will the bon. minister accept such rails ?

We will not accept any such under this contract.
Progress reported.
On motion of the Prime Minister, House adjourned at 11.45 p.m.

Wednesday, April 24, 1901.
